H.; Fotheringham, P.; Goodger, B.; Miller, E.; Haynes, L.; Woolfenden, S.; Eastwood, J.; Liu, H.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The George Institute for Global Health, Faculty of Medicine and Health, University of New South Wales, Sydney, Australia
after.abstract:
ObjectivesTo describe a multi-methods explanatory evaluation protocol for Healthy Homes and Neighbourhoods (HHAN), an integrated care initiative for families experiencing health and social disadvantage in a Sydney health district. The evaluation will examine how and in what contexts HHAN influences health and social outcomes and will assess its value for money.

DesignMulti-methods explanatory evaluation using linked administrative data, realist-informed interviews, yarning, and economic evaluation.

SettingA Sydney health district, including place-based hubs and partner sites involved in HHAN delivery or support.

ParticipantsFor the quantitative analyses, study participants will include participants of the HHAN program, linked family members in the Human Services Dataset, and a constructed counterfactual population. For the qualitative interviews and yarning, study participants will include service providers, program managers, policymakers, clients and carers involved in the HHAN program, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander participants where culturally appropriate and approved.

Methods and analysisImpact on health and social outcomes will be examined using linked administrative data with matching, weighting and regression-based approaches. A critical realist analysis of interview and yarning transcripts will explore program mechanisms of change and implementation conditions. Economic evaluation will estimate return on investment and cost-effectiveness where data permit. Findings will be integrated to explain patterns of impact and implementation across contexts.

Strengths and limitations of this protocolO_LIThis protocol describes an approach that combines linked administrative data, qualitative interviews, yarning, and economic evaluation to explain not only whether the HHAN program is associated with outcomes, but how, why, and in what contexts outcomes may occur.
C_LIO_LIThe design embeds Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander leadership, an Aboriginal Advisory Committee and culturally grounded methods, supporting cultural safety, data sovereignty and interpretation at a knowledge interface.
C_LIO_LIUse of a counterfactual population, weighting, regression modelling and sensitivity analyses strengthens causal interpretation within the constraints of a non-randomised real-world evaluation.
C_LIO_LIAs an observational evaluation conducted in open service systems, residual confounding, data linkage constraints and incomplete administrative data may limit the precision and generalisability of some estimates.
C_LIO_LIEconomic analyses will depend on the availability, completeness and comparability of cost and outcome data across government, health system and societal perspectives.
C_LI

after.abstract: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) represents approximately 20% of all skin cancers and is rising in global incidence. Although cSCC is known to progress from chronically sun-damaged keratinocytes via premalignant actinic keratosis (AK), the underlying spatial and molecular dynamics remain poorly defined. Here, we applied Xenium single-cell spatial transcriptomics to whole-skin sections from AK (n = 2) and cSCC (n = 2) patients to map key transitions in cSCC development. We resolved four distinct cSCC tumor cell subpopulations--epithelial, secretory, invasive, and stressed--whose transcriptional profiles diverge from bulk cSCC as well as normal and activated keratinocytes. Notably, we identified a METhigh tumor subpopulation, potentially linked to aggressive disease progression and resistance to immune checkpoint inhibition.

after.title: Preprint: A deep multimodal model for age-related macular degeneration detection using optical coherence tomography imaging and clinical text data
after.authors: Fang, M.; Miri, H.; Bishop, K.; Robatjazy, D.; Ko, R. C.; Nrusimhadevara, R.; Cayabyab, F. S.; Ko, S.-B.; Taghibiglou, C.
after.abstract: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a major cause of vision loss, with a significant impact on the elderly population worldwide. Machine learning and deep learning methods, combined with optical coherence tomography (OCT), are promising for the rapid diagnosis of AMD. However, most models focus only on one single OCT imaging modality or neglect clinical information. To improve this problem, we design a deep multimodal framework that integrates OCT images with clinical text data for the detection of AMD. Then, we evaluate the proposed model using metrics, such as accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, F-score, and the area under the curve (AUC), achieving excellent detection results at both the image level and patient level. Next, we conduct computational efficiency analysis and independent external validation to further demonstrate the efficiency and generalizability of the proposed model. In addition, we provide visualization results with explainable AI technique to further show the effectiveness of the proposed model. Our proposed model using multimodal strategy involving machine learning along with available clinical text and OCT imaging data accurately predicts individuals with AMD. Therefore, the use of machine learning and explainable AI in AMD detection may ultimately improve early diagnosis and offer more precise and personalized treatment strategies, improving the management of AMD and preserving vision.

after.title: Preprint: Rethink the Flow: Establishing a Preanalytical Workflow for Protein Detection in Menstrual Effluent.
after.authors: Denuga, S.; Lukaszczyk, B.; Okwuegbuna, T.; Suryoharaharjo, K.; Ogata, A.
after.abstract: BACKGROUND: Menstrual effluent (ME) is a promising, minimally invasive biofluid that contains unique protein biomarkers indicative of systemic and gynecological health. Despite its potential, the adoption of ME as a biofluid for disease identification remains limited because no standardized protocols exist for sample collection, processing, and storage. The lack of standardization remains a major challenge in ME research, introducing non-biological variability that limits accurate protein measurements and downstream interpretation for disease diagnosis. We examine how preanalytical factors, including centrifugation, freeze-thaw cycling, and pre-processing storage conditions, affect sample stability and protein concentration measurements. METHODS: Single-molecule array (Simoa) technology was used to quantify cancer antigen 125 (CA125) in ME samples collected from 19 participants. RESULTS: We found that delays in sample processing beyond eight hours increased the probability of unsuccessful fractionation (p < 0.02), a metric of sample stability. We detected CA125 in 100% of ME and ME-derived plasma samples; however, plasma showed better reproducibility across aliquots. Repeated freeze-thaw cycling significantly altered CA125 concentrations in plasma samples. ME samples stored at 4 {degrees} C before centrifugation maintained their ability to fractionate and protein integrity for up to 120 h. We also demonstrate that the developed workflow is compatible with longitudinal monitoring of CA125 in ME over three consecutive cycles. CONCLUSIONS: These results support at-home self-collection of ME for sample acquisition. Furthermore, the developed workflow enabled reliable protein biomarker analysis, facilitating the use of ME as a biofluid for biomarker discovery for gynecological diseases.

after.title: Preprint: Impaired Skeletal Muscle Glucose Handling in Patients with Advanced Stage Lung Cancer Is Improved by Exercise Training Despite Blunted Molecular Plasticity
after.authors: Carl, C. S.; Madsen, A. M. H.; Sorensen, J.; Hahn, N. J.; Andersen, N. R.; Lindqvist, C. B.; Damgaard, A.; Suhr, M.; Mfeketo, M. K.; Hjorth, M. A. B.; Hoegh, S. E.; Lillelund, C.; Quist, M.; Richter, E. A.; Sylow, L.
after.abstract:
BackgroundPatients with lung cancer often exhibit impaired glycemic control and insulin resistance, which are associated with poor clinical outcomes and increased mortality. However, skeletal muscle insulin sensitivity and the potential of exercise training to improve muscle glucose handling remain undetermined in these patients.

MethodsTen patients with advanced stage lung cancer and 12 matched controls completed five weeks of one-legged knee-extension exercise training. Whole-body and leg insulin sensitivity were assessed by a hyperinsulinemic-euglycemic clamp with femoral arterio-venous catheterization and blood flow measurements. Muscle biopsies from both legs, obtained before and during insulin stimulation, were analyzed for glycogen, protein abundance, and insulin signaling.

ResultsCompared with controls, patients had lower whole-body insulin sensitivity (-24%, p=0.030), leg glucose extraction (-37%, p=0.030), and muscle glycogen (-15%, p=0.045). Training increased leg glucose uptake (26%, p<0.001), blood flow (17%, p=0.005), and glycogen (32%, p<0.001) across both groups. Protein abundance did not differ between groups in the non-trained leg. Training increased GLUT4, Akt2, GSK3{beta}, and AMPK2 across both groups, whereas HKII and TBC1D4 increased only in controls, resulting in a 61% smaller overall molecular training response in patients (composite protein score, p=0.004). Training-induced changes in leg glucose uptake correlated with changes in GLUT4 levels (r=0.46, p=0.042). Insulin-stimulated phosphorylation of AktSer473, GSK3{beta}Ser9, and TBC1D4Thr642 did not differ between groups.

ConclusionsAdvanced stage lung cancer is associated with impaired whole-body and skeletal muscle glucose handling. Exercise training was effective in increasing muscle glucose uptake in these patients, although blunted molecular adaptations may limit the full metabolic benefit.

after.title: Preprint: Does altering antiretroviral therapy impact an individual's gut microbiome?
after.authors: Lindergard, G.; Mann, E.; MacDonald, M.; Ustianowski, A.
after.abstract:
IntroductionPeople with HIV are living with increased chronic inflammation with gut microbiome dysbiosis and microbial translocation emerging as contributing factors to inflammation and development of HIV associated co-morbidities. Single time-point cross-sectional population studies of individuals on antiretroviral drug therapy have suggested that some classes of antiretroviral therapy (ART) affect the gut microbiome more than others. There is, however, a lack of data examining the microbiome changes prospectively in individuals before and after alteration of their antiretroviral regiment. This study prospectively assesses changes in individuals bacterial gut microbiome when switching from one antiretroviral drug or delivery method to another class or delivery method.

MethodsWe conducted an observational prospective study of the gut microbiome in virologically controlled HIV infected individuals who were going through a planned switch of their ART regimen. We enrolled 15 participants and stool samples were collected before and 3-6 weeks after the switch of ART and analysed via shallow shotgun metagenomics.

ResultsWe did not detect a statistically significant overall difference in microbiome perturbation between the study participant group that switched their antiretroviral therapy compared to the controls who continued with the same ART during the timeframe of the study. Though underpowered to detect changes in subgroups, a noticeable observational shift in the 20 most abundant bacterial species was seen when individuals changed from a protease inhibitor-based regime to a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI) based regimen. Individuals who changed from NNRTI based treatment to integrase inhibitor-based treatment and from integrase inhibitor-based ART to protease inhibitor-based ART demonstrated numerical changes and shifts that failed to meet statistical significance. The initiation of intramuscular delivery of ART and a move away from oral drug did not result in a significant shift in the bacterial community in stool samples in this limited number of individuals.

ConclusionWe did not see statistically significant changes that were larger than those observed in controls in this small study. Switching from protease inhibitor to NNRTI demonstrated the largest shift in bacterial species that had been previously associated with positive health outcomes, indicating that protease inhibitor-based regimen might have a negative effect on the gut microbiome. Further larger prospective studies are planned to explore this area.

after.title: Preprint: Comparing the Natural Decline of Carbon Monoxide (CO) Levels Using Four Breath CO Monitors Among Hospitalized Daily Tobacco Smokers: Implications for Determining Abstinence in Smoking Cessation Clinical Trials
after.authors: Wagner, W. P.; Smith, B.; Long, D. P.; Thomas, S. J.; Businelle, M.; Gamble, K. L.; Cropsey, K. L.
after.abstract: Biochemical verification of smoking outcomes is standard for determining the efficacy of treatments in smoking cessation clinical trials. The most common, cost-effective, and non-invasive biochemical verification method is breath carbon monoxide (CO) monitoring. No studies have examined the natural course of CO reduction in forced abstinence settings over multiple days with multiple devices to determine optimal cutoffs. This project compared the four most commonly used CO monitors (Vitalograph BreathCO, piCO+, iCOquit [corded and Bluetooth]) across 44 hours of monitoring on an inpatient hospital unit for 26 participants who reported daily cigarette smoking. Linear mixed models were used to fit smooth curves and control within subject correlations. Receiver operator characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed using logistic regression to examine performance of different cut-offs for CO for each device using sensitivity, specificity, Youdens J, area under the curve (AUC), and efficiency. By the end of monitoring (>40 hours), 100% of participants had a <3 ppm on Vitalograph BreathCO. Using the Vitalograph BreathCO as the gold standard, both the bluetooth and corded iCOquits had an optimal cutoff of <3 ppm, while the piCO+ had an optimal cutoff of <5 ppm. CO monitors demonstrated different cutoffs and should not be used interchangeably. Cutoffs higher than 5 ppm should not be used to indicate abstinence, regardless of CO device.

after.authors: Laker, M.; O'Mara, T. A.; Spurdle, A. B.; Tischkowitz, M.; Pharoah, P. A.; Davidson, E. J.; Easton, D.; Antoniou, A. C.; Yang, X.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Centre for Cancer Genetic Epidemiology, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK
after.abstract:
BackgroundEndometrial cancer is the most common gynaecological malignancy in high-income countries, yet its genetic architecture remains incompletely understood. While pathogenic variants in mismatch repair genes are well-established contributors, the role of rare variants in other genes has not been systematically characterized.

MethodsWe evaluated associations between rare genetic variants and endometrial cancer risk based on 2,675 cases and 160,654 controls from the UK Biobank and the 100,000 Genomes Project. Gene-level associations were assessed using burden tests, with protein-truncating variants (PTVs) and missense variants (MSVs) predicted to be deleterious analysed separately.

ResultsEndometrial cancer (EC) risk associations were observed for three established EC susceptibility genes in the rare PTV analysis: MSH6 (RR = 36.6, 95% CI 25.9-51.8), MLH1 (RR = 52.5, 95% CI 21.3-129.4) and MSH2 (RR = 13.0, 95% CI 6.0-28.2). In the rare MSV analysis, PTEN was also significantly associated with EC risk (RR = 9.7, 95% CI 4.0-23.7). Beyond these established susceptibility genes, exome-wide significance was observed for 19 additional genes in the PTV analysis, including PHKG2 (RR = 29.8, 95% CI 9.6-92.8), and eight additional genes in the MSV analysis.

ConclusionThis study identifies novel candidate genes associated with endometrial cancer risk, providing a foundation for future replication studies.

after.abstract:
Synopsis

BackgroundDoxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxyPEP) reduces the incidence of bacterial sexually transmitted infections, but its impact on antimicrobial susceptibility among bystander bacteria remains unclear.

ObjectivesTo assess changes in susceptibility to doxycycline among rectal Escherichia coli after 6 months of doxyPEP. Secondary objectives assessed susceptibility for other classes of antimicrobials and in other species.

Patients and methodsSingle-centre, open-label, single-arm trial at an HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis clinic in Belgium. Participants used doxycycline 200mg within 72h after condomless sex for 180 days. Anorectal swabs and oral rinse samples were collected at baseline and day 180. Susceptibility was assessed by disc diffusion on six colonies per species. Differences in inhibition-zone diameters were analysed using censored Bayesian mixed-effects Gaussian regression.

ResultsSeventy-nine participants were enrolled, 73 completed day 180. Among rectal isolates, cefixime inhibition-zone diameters decreased in E. coli and Klebsiella spp., other estimates were imprecise. Among oral isolates, inhibition-zone diameters decreased for doxycycline and azithromycin in streptococci, staphylococci and commensal Neisseria spp.; ceftriaxone and cefixime in commensal Neisseria spp.; and ciprofloxacin and penicillin in staphylococci and commensal Neisseria spp. Ceftriaxone inhibition-zone diameters increased in oral streptococci. Sensitivity analyses were broadly consistent. Twenty-five participants experienced drug-related adverse events, none serious.

ConclusionsSix months of doxyPEP was associated with reduced susceptibility to doxycycline and several other antimicrobials, predominantly among oral bacteria. Rectal findings were less precise apart from reduced cefixime susceptibility in E. coli and Klebsiella spp. These findings support further studies of DoxyPEP and bystander selection across multiple bacterial taxa and antimicrobial classes.

after.title: Preprint: Temporal and Geographic Variation in Humidity as an Effect Modifier of the Association Between Heatwaves and Mental Health-Related Emergency Department Visits Among Medicaid Beneficiaries in the U.S. Gulf States
after.authors: Ramesh, B.; Luglio, D.; Wellenius, G. A.; Hossain, C. A.; Al-Zubayer, M. A.; Monis, R. P.; Rahman, M. M.
after.abstract: With projected increases in humid heat, the extent to which humidity modifies the association between heatwaves and acute mental health (MH) outcomes is important but remains understudied. We evaluated this effect modification using Medicaid claims data on MH-related emergency department (ED) visits (2012-2019). The analysis included 14 million MH-related ED visits across five U.S. Gulf states, aggregated to county-weeks. Heatwave weeks were defined as weeks with daily maximum temperatures above the county-specific 97th percentile for [≥]2 consecutive days. Following a county-level self-matched design, heatwave weeks were matched to non-heatwave weeks in the same calendar weeks of a randomly selected year. Conditional quasi-Poisson regression models estimated rate ratios (RRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs), with interactions assessing effect modification by weekly and county-level climatological humidity in separate models. Heatwave weeks were associated with higher rates of any MH-related ED visits (RR, 1.11; 95% CI, 1.09-1.12), including visits for substance use disorders, anxiety disorders, and depression. Associations were 7% and 5% stronger during high- and very-high-humidity weeks, respectively, than during low-humidity weeks indicating effect modification by humidity. These findings support incorporating humidity into heat-health interventions to better target populations and periods with heightened risk to reduce the MH burden associated with heatwaves.

after.title: Preprint: Co-occurrence Is Not Evidence: Separating Protein-Disease Findings from Incidental Mentions in HFpEF Literature
after.authors: Azat, A.; De Santana Junior, C. J.; Cadeiras, M.; Liem, D. A.
after.abstract:
Literature-mining pipelines such as CaseOLAP rank proteins by how often they appear next to a disease term. Appearing next to a disease is not the same as being implicated in it: in our 300-sentence held-out set of PubMed sentences that mention a protein and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), only 115 assert a biological association. The rest report a negative finding or mention the protein in passing, for example as a drug the patients were taking. We train a sentence-level filter that sorts each protein mention into associated, not_associated or incidental. It is a fine-tuned PubMedBERT trained with class-weighted cross-entropy and R-Drop regularization, combined into a six-model majority-vote ensemble over three random seeds. On the held-out set, with no thresholds tuned on it, the ensemble reaches 85.3% accuracy and 86.1% macro F1 (bootstrap 95% confidence intervals 81.0-89.3% and 82.1-89.7%), against 38.3% accuracy for the co-occurrence baseline, which counts every mention as an association. Single models average 84.4 {+/-} 0.7% accuracy across seeds. Run after CaseOLAP, the filter removes protein mentions that are not evidence of association from the HFpEF candidate list.

Where the ensembles majority vote disagreed with the annotation, the annotation was often wrong. Expert review of those sentences corrected 53 of 88 flagged evaluation labels and 109 training labels. Most of the errors came from one flaw in the annotation sheet: in sentences naming several proteins, it did not say which protein the label was for. The audit stage coincided with the largest accuracy gain in the project, but the same stage also changed the evaluation labels and the training loss, so we report it as a chronology, not as a controlled result.

after.title: Preprint: Modelling the impact of a school-based influenza vaccination programme under uncertainty in seasonal transmission dynamics
after.authors: Boksenbojm, E.; Eales, O.; Cheng, A. C.; McCaw, J.; Shearer, F. M.
after.abstract: School-aged children are thought to be an important driver of influenza transmission. In this paper we study the direct and indirect health effects of a school-based live-attenuated influenza vaccination (LAIV) programme in Australia, using a stochastic, age-stratified model of seasonal influenza transmission. The model was calibrated using Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) in order to capture uncertainty in influenza infection dynamics. The calibrated model was used to evaluate programmes varying in target age group, vaccination coverage and vaccine effectiveness. On average, school-based LAIV programmes reduced infections and hospitalisations at the population level across all scenarios, with greater reductions at higher coverage and vaccine effectiveness and when both primary- and secondary-school-aged children were targeted. However, estimated effects varied substantially across plausible transmission dynamics, particularly indirect effects -- for some programme scenarios, we estimated that in non-target age groups both near complete suppression or a small increase in infections were possible outcomes. For all scenarios, we estimated that school-based LAIV programmes would lead to a reduction in infections and hospitalisations in target age groups.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Partitioning lifespan inequality in hierarchical study designs with an application to global healthy longevity

after.title: Preprint: Partitioning lifespan inequality in hierarchical study designs with an application to global healthy longevity
after.authors: Caswell, H.
after.abstract:
BackgroundDemographic inequality arises from two sources: heterogeneity among individuals subject to different rates, and stochastic variation among individuals subject to identical rates. Partitioning lifespan inequality into these components has been limited to heterogeneity in single factors or, very recently, factorial study designs with multiple factors. Methods for hierarchical designs have been lacking.

ObjectivesThe goal of this paper is to present a generally applicable method to partition inequality of lifespan (and other demographic outcomes) into components within and between levels in a hierarchical study design.

MethodsThe analysis treats a heterogeneous population as a mixture distribution. Inequality is measured by the variance and partitioned into components between groups (e.g., geographical or economic regions), between sub-groups within groups (e.g., countries within regions), and stochasticity within sub-groups. The method is applied to global inequality in healthy longevity, using data for 194 countries from the Global Burden of Disease study, divided into four regions according to the World Bank income categories and into countries within each region. Results are compared for flat and population-weighted mixing distributions.

ResultsThe protocol for variance partitioning in hierarchical study designs provides variance among regions, among countries within regions, and within countries. It extends naturally to multiple levels (e.g., states within countries) and to factorial components (e.g., regions defined by combinations of income and education). When applied to global healthy longevity, the dominant source of inequality is stochastic variation within countries, which accounts for 85%-95% of the overall inequality. The population-weighted mixing distribution reduces the contribution of between-group variance.

ContributionSome of the largest demographic data sets have a hierarchical organization. The methods presented here make it possible to partition inequality, measured by variance, in such studies.

after.title: Preprint: What Does an Agent-Run Clinic Cost? Protocol for a Prospective Observational Study of the Compute Cost of Completed Work in a Clinical Agent Fleet
after.authors: Elalfy, O.; Youssef, S.; Davids, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Wai Health Inc, Palo Alto, CA, United States
after.abstract: Background: Decisions about deploying large language model (LLM) agents in health care require the cost of completed work in production. Published evidence reports benchmark accuracy, benchmark-level cost, and time or financial outcomes for ambient documentation, and list prices alone do not determine the cost of completed work. To our knowledge, no deployed clinical agent fleet has published a measurement method that ties compute cost, latency, failures and retries to completed work. Objective: This study aims to estimate the compute cost of completed work by the orchestrated clinical agents of a deployed LLM agent fleet over a 12-week window of production telemetry, using estimators, data-quality gates and an analysis plan fixed before any window data are extracted for the study. Methods: The setting is a private outpatient clinic in London, United Kingdom, where wai, a multi-agent system supporting clinic operations, is deployed. The population is every run of the 20 orchestrated clinical documentation and decision-support agents starting between September 21 and December 13, 2026. The run store writes 2 records for every run, a non-terminal record before the model call and a terminal record after it, and has no attempt counter or parent-run link. Estimators defined on that structure cover cost per resolved execution and per completed intention, retry and failed-intention shares of compute, error and failure rates, latency, cost per draft offered for clinician review and a latency-cost frontier, by agent, task class and acceptance stratum. Cost is recorded in GBP pence, converted from provider-returned US dollar cost at a fixed rate and rounded per model call. The plan fixes weekly aggregation, small-cell suppression, bootstrap intervals over weeks, 2 prespecified comparisons, 5 sensitivity analyses and 4 data-quality gates whose failure converts an estimate into a bound or an unmeasured stratum. Two staff-level measures proposed during planning were dropped. Revenue, pricing, margin and staffing inference are excluded. Results: The measurement window opened on September 21, 2026, and closes on December 13, 2026, and telemetry is being recorded in routine operation. No window data had been extracted for this study at submission. Aggregate whole-table counts that include window records were extracted on November 19, 2026, for companion manuscripts and are disclosed. Extraction will begin no earlier than December 15, 2026, and the results are expected to be submitted for publication in 2027. Conclusions: The compute cost of completed clinical agent work can be specified as estimators over the run-level telemetry this deployment records, provided paired recording rows are separated from retries, missing terminal states are bounded and rounding of recorded cost is reported. This protocol fixes those estimators, and the reporting consequence of each known instrumentation defect, before extraction. Trial Registration: None. The analysis plan will be registered on Open Science Framework Registries before any window data are extracted for this study. International Registered Report Identifier (IRRID): DERR1-10.2196/ (to be assigned by the journal)

Methods: The setting is a private outpatient clinic in London, United Kingdom, where wai, a multi-agent system supporting clinic operations, is deployed. The population is every run of the 20 orchestrated clinical documentation and decision-support agents starting between September 21 and December 13, 2026. The run store writes 2 records for every run, a non-terminal record before the model call and a terminal record after it, and has no attempt counter or parent-run link. Estimators defined on that structure cover cost per resolved execution and per completed intention, retry and failed-intention shares of compute, error and failure rates, latency, cost per draft offered for clinician review and a latency-cost frontier, by agent, task class and acceptance stratum. Cost is recorded in GBP pence, converted from provider-returned US dollar cost at a fixed rate and rounded per model call. The plan fixes weekly aggregation, small-cell suppression, bootstrap intervals over weeks, 2 prespecified comparisons, 5 sensitivity analyses and 4 data-quality gates whose failure converts an estimate into a bound or an unmeasured stratum. Two staff-level measures in an earlier version were dropped. Revenue, pricing, margin and staffing inference are excluded. Results: The measurement window opened on September 21, 2026, and closes on December 13, 2026, and telemetry is being recorded in routine operation. No window data had been extracted for this study at submission. Aggregate whole-table counts that include window records were extracted on November 19, 2026, for companion manuscripts and are disclosed. Extraction will begin no earlier than December 15, 2026, and the results are expected to be submitted for publication in 2027. Conclusions: The compute cost of completed clinical agent work can be specified as estimators over the run-level telemetry this deployment records, provided paired recording rows are separated from retries, missing terminal states are bounded and rounding of recorded cost is reported. This protocol fixes those estimators, and the reporting consequence of each known instrumentation defect, before extraction. Trial Registration: None. The analysis plan will be registered on Open Science Framework Registries before any window data are extracted for this study.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Wai Health Inc, Palo Alto, CA, United States
after.abstract: Objective. Guidance for large language model (LLM) drafting in clinical care relies on human review, yet review is rarely measured as a control. We aimed to define computable measures of review fidelity, establish which a deployed system can compute, and pre-specify their first analysis. Materials and Methods. For a multi-agent clinical system in routine use at one private London outpatient clinic, we defined acceptance coverage, attribution completeness, the unedited acceptance rate (UAR), a bounded normalized edit distance, availability latency and an unedited fast-approval rate (UFA). We checked each measure against the system's code and database structure at a fixed commit on four approval routes and pre-specified a prospective 12-week analysis. Results. The UAR equals the mass at zero of the edit-distance distribution, and availability latency bounds reading time from above only. Clinical documentation keeps draft and signed text with a recorded signer, so the core measures are computable there. Help-desk edit telemetry is written only when the agent's version has been stored. The WhatsApp agent route records no edit signal, and its approver need not be named. No route records when a draft is opened. Documentation accept events were not written before a change committed on November 16, 2026. Model-generated content, including live voice-agent speech, also reaches patients without approval. No measured values are reported. Discussion. Acceptance alone cannot separate accurate drafts from approval without reading, and three of four routes cannot yet support the family. Conclusion. Review fidelity can be specified as telemetry at the approval event. Validation against missed errors is required.

after.authors: Lazari, A.; Broulidakis, J.; Gillis, G.; Bhalerao, G.; Halls, D.; Wickham, F.; Tendler, B. C.; Sotiropoulos, S. N.; Griffanti, L.; Husain, M.; Mars, R. B.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Oxford Centre for Integrative Neuroimaging (OxCIN), FMRIB, Nuffield Department of Clinical Neurosciences, University of Oxford
after.abstract: Background: Neurodegenerative disorders are common in ageing populations, and arise from several distinct pathophysiological causes. Yet, they also share many symptoms, including cognitive and neuropsychiatric ones. It is unclear to what extent the impact of neurodegeneration on brain systems is unique or shared across disorders, and whether shared symptoms are driven by degeneration of the same brain systems. Methods: We collected data from n=251 participants with Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease, Small Vessel Disease, and age-matched healthy controls. All participants underwent harmonized cognitive and neuropsychiatric assessment and were scanned using the UK-Biobank MRI protocol capturing features including brain volume, white matter lesions and microstructure, tract volume, iron content, and functional connectivity. Results: We replicated established case-control brain changes in Alzheimer's Disease, Parkinson's Disease and Small Vessel Disease compared to healthy controls. Leveraging this joint standardised dataset, we identified distinct neuroimaging features of individual neurodegenerative disorders, providing evidence for robust diagnosis-specific brain changes. Importantly, however, there was also a large degree of transdiagnostic similarity across neuroimaging markers. Testing for transdiagnostic associations between symptoms and brain phenotypes, we found that lower medial frontal pole connectivity to primary motor cortex was preferentially associated with apathy, fatigue, and depression; whereas cingulum microstructure was associated with cognitive deficits across diagnoses. Conclusions: These results demonstrate that different neurodegenerative diseases are characterised by dissociable brain changes, but also common transdiagnostic and symptom-associated features. This suggests that shared symptoms across neurodegeneration may in part be driven by overlapping impact on key brain systems, such as changes in medial frontal pole connectivity and cingulum microstructure. Our work highlights that multimodal imaging biomarkers can help understand and parse symptomatic heterogeneity in neurodegenerative and ageing populations.

after.abstract: Advances in ultrasensitive proteomics offer opportunities to characterize molecular pathways underlying brain aging. We measured 220 plasma proteins using NULISAseq Neuro220 in 250 Chinese, South Asian, and non-Hispanic White older adults (mean age=68.2 years, 70.4% female). Proteins implicated in neurodegenerative diseases (including brain-derived phosphorylated Tau, BDpTau), synaptic function, oxidative stress, and inflammation were associated with poorer cognition. Phosphorylated Tau205 was associated with reduced entorhinal thickness, whereas inflammatory proteins were associated with imaging markers of cerebral small vessel disease. Several findings were replicated in 1,381 participants in the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, including associations of BDpTau species, NPTX2, BACE1, TREM1, CCL17, PRDX6, and IGF1R with cognitive decline and clinical progression. Cardiometabolic risk factors were associated with widespread proteomic alterations, many of which were also linked to poorer brain health. These results identify promising molecular markers of brain aging and extend proteomic research to ethnically diverse populations historically underrepresented in Alzheimer's disease research.

after.authors: Horisawa, S.; Fukui, A.; Kim, K.; Taira, T.; Miyao, S.
after.abstract: How focal subthalamic injury disrupts a distributed arousal system remains incompletely understood. We investigated transient somnolence after unilateral pallidothalamic tractotomy without sedation in 56 patients, including 14 with somnolence. Volume-adjusted probabilistic lesion mapping identified a hotspot dorsal to the lateral hypothalamus (MNI -6.0, -10.5, -4.0 mm; family-wise error-corrected P = 0.011). A model combining peak involvement and log-transformed lesion volume achieved a leave-one-out cross-validated area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.799. Applied without refitting to two external cohorts comprising 19 patients, it achieved an AUC of 0.830 (95% confidence interval 0.636-0.977; two-sided cohort-stratified exact permutation P = 0.0166). In a supplementary analysis, somnolence-associated lesions had greater map-weighted burden within a published structural connectivity map of consciousness recovery after deep brain stimulation (P = 0.0299). These findings identify a focal subthalamic vulnerability in maintaining human wakefulness, with a lesion-based model discriminating transient somnolence in independent surgical patients.

after.authors: Kulkarni, D. D.; Toivonen, A. R.; Luddy, A.; Reiling, S.; Thornton, J.; Hoche, F.; Gupta, A. S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA
after.abstract: Background: Ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T) is a rare, childhood-onset neurodegenerative disorder for which sensitive, age-appropriate motor outcome measures are needed to support emerging clinical trials. Clinician-rated ataxia scales are limited by subjectivity, low granularity, and floor and ceiling effects. We evaluated whether at-home wearable accelerometry, combined with machine-learned composite scores derived from submovement features, captures cross-sectional motor impairment and longitudinal disease progression in A-T. Methods: 43 children with classic A-T (median age 9.0 years; IQR 5.7-13.4) and 50 age- and sex-matched controls wore GENEActiv accelerometers on the ankle and wrist during one week of natural behavior at home, repeated at 6- to 12-month intervals. From 85 submovement, activity-intensity, and spectral features per sensor site, we trained composite severity models targeting the Brief Ataxia Rating Scale (BARS) gait subscore (ankle) and BARS total score (wrist). Findings: Ankle composite scores correlated strongly with BARS gait (r = 0.88), BARS total (r = 0.88), and caregiver-reported CPCHILD (r = -0.69); wrist composite scores correlated with BARS total (r = 0.88), BARS arm (r = 0.84), and CPCHILD (r = -0.78). Both models discriminated A-T from controls with large effect sizes (ankle Cohen's d = 2.28; wrist d = 2.98) and demonstrated excellent within-week reliability (ICC = 0.95 ankle; 0.92 wrist). The ankle composite captured disease progression sensitively (Mean-to-Standard Deviation Ratio [MSDR] = 0.98; p < 0.0001). In a matched subset with both sensor and clinical data, ankle composite slopes significantly captured progression (Wilcoxon vs zero, p = 0.0036), whereas BARS total (p = 0.079) and BARS gait (p = 0.30) did not. Interpretation: At-home ankle-based wearable accelerometry provides a sensitive, interpretable, and ecologically valid measure of motor function and disease progression in A-T and may serve as a candidate outcome measure for clinical trials.

after.abstract: Introduction: Stroma areactive invasion front areas (SARIFA) are a histopathological phenomenon at the tumour invasion front characterised by direct tumour-adipocyte contact (TAC). It can be detected on histological Haematoxylin-Eosin (H&E) stained tumour slides. TAC/SARIFA has emerged as a strong negative prognostic factor in several tumour entities. In this monocentric retrospective study, we aim to elucidate the impact of TAC/SARIFA in oropharyngeal cancer. Materials and methods: 78 cases of pT3 to pT4 oropharyngeal squamous cell cancer from 2005 to 2023 and their corresponding lymph nodes were analysed for the occurrence of TAC/SARIFA. Besides, we compared overall survival rates, recurrence-free survival (RFS) and association with biological and pathological tumour characteristics. Results: In total, overall survival was significantly reduced in TAC/SARIFA-positive tumours (p=0.014). Moreover, TAC/SARIFA positive primary tumours are associated with TAC/SARIFA positive lymph nodes (p<0.001) and extranodal extension (ENE) (p=0.032). Finally, RFS in TAC/SARIFA-positive tumours was reduced, but not significantly (p=0.072). No significant difference was found between p16 positive and p16 negative tumours and prevalence of TAC/SARIFA. Conclusion: TAC/SARIFA is a possible prognostically relevant risk factor in oropharyngeal cancer. When detected in the primary tumour or lymph nodes, it is associated with reduced overall survival rates and tendency towards shorter RFS. TAC/SARIFA-positive lymph nodes almost always show ENE.

after.authors: Song, J.; Kim, E.; Amar, A. K.; Chavarriaga Soto, J.; Raman, J. D.; Herrera-Caceres, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Penn State Health Milton S. Hershey Medical Center
after.abstract: Background: Among transplant candidates with kidney failure attributed to renal cell carcinoma (RCC), we investigated whether deceased-donor kidney transplantation was associated with longer survival than continued waiting and whether the association varied by kidney donor profile index (KDPI). Methods: We studied adult kidney-alone candidates listed in 2005-2025 in the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network registry (follow-up through March 31, 2026) whose coded cause of kidney failure was RCC, versus all other candidates. Time-dependent Cox models compared transplantation with waiting. Calendar-aligned sequential trials with propensity overlap weighting estimated survival after transplantation with a KDPI [≤]85% kidney versus continued waiting. Results: Of 599,887 candidates, 1,542 had RCC-attributed kidney failure (614 deaths). Of these, 597 received a KDPI [≤]85% kidney and 38 received a KDPI >85% kidney. A KDPI [≤]85% transplant was associated with lower mortality than waiting (hazard ratio [HR] 0.51, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.42 to 0.62). The HR was 0.53 in other candidates (interaction P = 0.86). Five-year survival was 83.1% after transplantation and 67.0% with continued waiting (difference, 16.0 percentage points, 95% CI 11.8 to 20.1). The restricted mean survival time difference was 5.8 months (95% CI 4.4 to 7.4). For KDPI >85%, the HR was 1.65 (95% CI 0.87 to 3.13). Conclusions: Transplantation with a KDPI [≤]85% kidney was associated with about 16 additional survivors per 100 RCC candidates at 5 years. The estimate for KDPI >85% was imprecise. Tumor stage and cancer-free interval were unavailable.

after.abstract: Presurgical localization of the epileptogenic zone remains a central challenge in drug-resistant focal epilepsy. At the same time, the abundant interictal intracranial EEG (iEEG) data routinely acquired during presurgical evaluation remain an underexploited source of localizing information. We developed an iEEG implant topology-aware transformer that combines interictal iEEG features with electrode coordinates to predict resection targets. The model was trained exclusively on three public datasets (n = 476) and tested on cohorts from five independent centers across three countries (n = 216). In patients with favorable surgical outcomes (Engel I; n = 120), the median area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) was 0.71, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.92, outperforming interictal spike rate and clinically defined seizure-onset zone baselines in patients with favorable outcomes (P < 0.05 for both AUPRC and AUROC). Patients with unfavorable outcomes (Engel II-IV; n = 96) had lower prediction-resection alignment (median AUPRC, 0.42), and their highest confidence predictions were located farther from resected tissue (P = 0.005). These findings establish a generalizable framework that integrates neural activity and brain topology to identify epileptogenic tissue from interictal recordings, potentially improving surgical success rates and reducing reliance on resource-intensive seizure capture.

after.abstract: IMPORTANCE Monitoring hemoglobin oxygen saturation is a cornerstone of patient care across a wide range of clinical settings, with pulse oximetry remaining one of the most widely used technologies. Recent studies have identified skin pigmentation-related inaccuracies in these measurements; however, the biological and optical mechanisms underlying these limitations remain incompletely understood. OBJECTIVE To investigate the tissue compartments and wavelengths that drive skin pigmentation-related bias in oximetry using depth-resolved optoacoustic (OA) imaging. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS Prospective observational imaging study of n=46 healthy volunteers representing all 6 Fitzpatrick skin types (FST). EXPOSURES OA imaging of the tibialis anterior region during physiological oxygenation challenges induced by vascular occlusion, reperfusion, and exercise. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES A total of 3016 spatially resolved scans were obtained. Tissue compartments were segmented using a pretrained neural network. OA spectra, oxygen saturation estimates, responses to physiological interventions, and associations with skin pigmentation were evaluated across 41 wavelengths from 700 to 1100 nm. RESULTS Skin OA spectra closely mirrored the optical absorption characteristics of melanin, and OA signal intensities were strongly associated with FST, demonstrating a substantial influence of pigmentation on superficial oximetry measurements. Epidermal oxygen saturation estimates exhibited minimal changes during physiological interventions, especially in darkly pigmented skin. Skin signals showed pronounced associations with melanin-sensitive wavelengths, enabling FST classification based on optoacoustic skin signals. Pigmentation-related bias was greatest at shorter wavelengths and progressively decreased at longer wavelengths. In contrast, oxygenation measurements obtained from skeletal muscle were less affected by skin type and showed the strongest responses to vascular occlusion, reperfusion, and exercise. Depth-resolved OA imaging demonstrated that physiologically meaningful oxygenation information emerged only after propagation beyond the avascular epidermis into deeper vascularized tissue compartments. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE The combination of appropriate anatomical targeting, optimized wavelength selection, and correction for optical attenuation may represent a promising strategy for mitigating skin-pigmentation-related bias in oximetry.

after.abstract: Aims: Aficamten, a novel cardiac myosin inhibitor recently approved in several regions for adults with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM), requires structured echocardiographic monitoring to assess for left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction (LVSD). We aimed to describe the incidence, severity, trajectory, and clinical correlates of LVSD during aficamten therapy in patients enrolled in FOREST-HCM. Methods: Serial echocardiographic examinations were performed to inform investigator-driven dose adjustments and safety monitoring. Patients were categorized by on-treatment LV ejection fraction (LVEF): any incidence of LVSD (<50%) or no LVSD (always >/=50%). A prespecified subgroup analysis evaluated patients with any LVEF >/=50% to <55%. Results: Among 410 patients (mean [SD] age 60.2 [12.8] years, 43.7% female), 12 (2.9%; exposure adjusted incidence rate [EAIR] 2.1/100 patient-years) developed LVSD (none with LVEF <40%); only one event was corroborated by the core laboratory. LVEF recovered to >/=50% in 10 (83.3%) patients after dose reduction and in one after transient interruption. One patient had persistent LVSD, having also experienced LVSD while receiving placebo in the parent study. Concurrent non-serious clinical heart failure occurred in two patients (0.5%; EAIR 0.3/100 patient-years), resolving in one, while the other (with prior LVSD on placebo) permanently discontinued aficamten. Additionally, 47 patients (11.5%; EAIR 8.8/100 patient-years) demonstrated LVEF >/=50% to <55% and remained on aficamten without dose reduction or associated adverse events. Conclusion: LVSD was infrequent, mild, reversible, and rarely associated with transient non-serious heart failure symptoms. LVEF >/=50% to <55% appeared clinically benign, supporting structured echocardiographic monitoring and individualized dose optimization.

after.title: Preprint: Stain-robust classification of Alzheimer's disease and chronic traumatic encephalopathy
after.authors: Xu, L.; Nwakamma, M.; Tilton, C.; Abdolmohammadi, B.; McKee, A.; Stein, T.; Cherry, J.; Mez, J.; Kolachalama, V. B.
after.abstract: Retrospective reassessment of archival brain banks provides opportunities to identify previously undocumented neuropathologies. However, limited tissue availability and preservation, together with differences in sampling and staining protocols across brain banks, can constrain the histological information available for analysis. This study investigated whether computational models can integrate complementary information across histological stains and retain discriminative information under incomplete stain availability. A deep learning model incorporating shared-specific feature modeling, cross-stain knowledge distillation, and random modality masking was developed and evaluated on 1,607 whole slide images from the dorsolateral frontal cortex of 602 donors across three cohorts. Using chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) and their comorbidity as a proof-of-principle application, our model achieved macro-averaged areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.899, 0.904, and 0.898 across three stain-defined groups, exceeding corresponding single-stain baselines. Discriminative performance was retained when each group's defining stain was withheld. Model-predicted disease probabilities were associated with neuropathological staging measures for AD and CTE, and spatial attribution patterns on the remaining stains were largely preserved under defining-stain masking. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of leveraging complementary and partially overlapping histopathological information under incomplete stain availability, providing a foundation for future computational studies across brain regions and brain banks.

after.title: Preprint: Impact of immune heterogeneity on antigenic evolution
after.authors: Willemsen, M. S.; Neher, R. A.; Rozhnova, G.
after.abstract: Antigenic evolution allows pathogens to escape pre-existing host immunity, but hosts differ in their immune histories because of population structure, demographic processes, and stochastic variation. Whether such immune heterogeneity promotes pathogen antigenic diversification remains poorly understood. We investigated how different sources of immune heterogeneity affect antigenic evolution. We developed a status-based multi-strain transmission model in which novel strains emerge stochastically within a tree-structured antigenic space. We examined immune heterogeneity arising from mixing between host subpopulations, aging, and stochastic variation in immune profiles, and evaluated its effects on strain coexistence and phylogenetic diversity. Limited mixing generated immune differences between host subpopulations, but increased phylogenetic diversity only under strong population separation. Aging alone had little effect on evolutionary dynamics but enhanced the effect of limited mixing on phylogenetic diversity. Stochastic immune variation promoted strain replacement rather than coexistence, primarily through variation in the overall susceptible population available to newly emerging strains. In general, immune heterogeneity alone does not necessarily promote antigenic diversification. Its effects depend on how immune differences are generated and maintained within the host population. More broadly, our findings highlight the importance of understanding how assumptions linking epidemiological and evolutionary processes shape the emergent dynamics of evolutionary-epidemiological models.

after.authors: Ashraf, A.; Saddique, M. A. B.; Sajid, M. S.; Anjum, S.; Rizwan, F.; Qasim, M. Z.
after.abstract: Background: Social media has become an important source of health information, including information about medicines. Exposure to medicine-related content may affect decisions to use medicines without professional consultation. Objective: To describe self-medication practices and social-media exposure among adults in Punjab, Pakistan, and explore associations between self-medication frequency and demographic, social-media-use, and attitudinal factors. Methods: A cross-sectional analytical survey was conducted among adults aged 18-60 years in Punjab between March and May 2026. The final analytic sample comprised 280 participants. A bilingual (Urdu/English) questionnaire assessed demographics, social-media use and health-content exposure, self-medication in the preceding six months, medicine categories, and attitudes. The questionnaire was reviewed by two clinical experts and piloted among 30 participants. Descriptive analyses, chi-square tests, and multinomial logistic regression were reported using IBM SPSS Statistics; significance was set at alpha = 0.05. Results: Self-medication frequency was reported as Rarely by 117 participants (41.8%), Frequently by 130 (46.4%), and More Often by 33 (11.8%). Fever medicines were reported by 179 participants (63.9%) and gastrointestinal medicines by 96 (34.3%); multiple-response medicine categories were not mutually exclusive. Instagram was the most frequently selected social-media platform. Advertisement recall differed across self-medication frequency groups (chi-square (22) = 35.28, p = .036). Belief that medicines shown in advertisements/posts were safe was associated with self-medication frequency (chi-square (4) = 14.26, p = .007), while perceived risk was not (chi-square (4) = 1.587, p = .811). The multinomial model's overall test was not statistically significant (chi-square (40) = 54.07, p = .068; Nagelkerke R2 = .205). Likelihood-ratio tests identified associations for daily social-media-use duration (chi-square (2) = 13.085, p = .001), age group (chi-square (6) = 14.930, p = .021), and perceived advertisement safety (chi-square (4) = 10.899, p = .028). Conclusion: Self-medication was commonly reported in this sample. Some social-media-use and advertising-attitude variables were associated with self-medication frequency, but the overall regression model was not statistically significant and the cross-sectional design cannot establish causality. Findings should be interpreted cautiously given the sample composition and reported data limitations.

after.title: Preprint: Large Language Model Extraction and Inference of Physician Global Assessment from Clinical Notes in Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
after.authors: Ong, M. S.; Yao, J.; Lee, S.; Savova, G.; Natter, M.
after.abstract: Background: The physician global assessment (PhGA) is a core outcome measure in juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) but is incompletely captured, even in clinical registries. We developed a large language model (LLM) approach that extracts explicitly documented PhGA from clinical narratives and infers a score where none is recorded. To our knowledge, this is the first study to address both tasks. Methods: We linked charts from 306 children with JIA at one center to the Childhood Arthritis and Rheumatology Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry (2016-2024). A structured prompt was developed on 100 randomly sampled charts, then evaluated on 400 charts from patients not represented in the development set. Extraction used GPT-5.2 within a HIPAA-compliant Azure environment. Registry-recorded PhGA served as the reference standard, with discordances adjudicated by a pediatric rheumatologist blinded to both sources. Agreement was assessed by intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC(2,1)), exact match, and mean absolute error (MAE). Results: Against registry values, ICC(2,1) was 0.87 (95% CI 0.85-0.89; n=400), with 70.5% exact agreement and MAE 0.363. Agreement was near-perfect for explicit extractions (n=190; ICC 0.99; 95% CI 0.98-0.99) and lower for inferred scores (n=210; ICC 0.72; 95% CI 0.64-0.78). Large discordances ([≥]2 points) occurred in 7.3% of cases. Against the adjudicated standard, overall ICC(2,1) was 0.96 (95% CI 0.95-0.97), with 77.5% exact agreement and MAE 0.200. All 14 explicit discordances reflected mismatch between the registry and the clinical note, rather than extraction errors (adjudicated ICC 1.00). For inferred scores, ICC rose to 0.90 (95% CI 0.87-0.92). Residual disagreement was concentrated at the inactive/minimally active boundary. Conclusion: An LLM can reliably extract PhGA from clinical notes with high accuracy to support downstream clinical research, offering a scalable approach to mitigating missingness in patient registries.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Universidad del Desarrollo Facultad de Medicina
after.abstract: Background: Claims that an intervention is safe often rest on a nonsignificant difference, confusing absence of evidence with evidence of absence; an integrated, reproducible procedure for auditing them is lacking. We developed and evaluated one, applying it to diagnostic hysteroscopy in endometrial cancer, which published syntheses describe as oncologically safe. Methods and findings: The framework's eight steps verify each number, test the direction of confounding, require time-to-event analysis, bound detectability and apply one information-adjusted boundary to claims of harm and of safety (verdicts: harm established, safety established, inconclusive). The rule was fixed before a retrospective test on minimally invasive radical hysterectomy for cervical cancer, later assessed in a randomized trial, and evaluated analytically and by simulation. We audited 18 comparative studies of hysteroscopy, 12 with peritoneal cytology (4,078 patients) and 5 with time-to-event recurrence estimates. With a true hazard ratio (HR) of 1.25 and the information available for hysteroscopy, inferring safety from nonsignificance gave false reassurance in 34% of analyses and the rule in 1%; with adequate information and no harm, the rule established safety in 80%. Pre-trial evidence on minimally invasive radical hysterectomy proved inconclusive, not safe. For hysteroscopy, controlling for disease extent revealed an association with positive cytology (odds ratio 2.86, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.24-6.62) absent from crude comparisons; recurrence data (HR 1.17, Hartung-Knapp 95% CI 0.90-1.52) held 71% of the required information and were inconclusive at margins from 1.10 to 1.40; and harm through cytology would be undetectable in low-risk disease. Limitations include development on the case to which it is applied, a retrospective test of author-selected evidence, and reliance on published observational data. Conclusions: The framework distinguishes evidence of absence from absence of evidence in claims of safety and can be applied with a published confidence interval in minutes. It provides a reproducible, low-barrier procedure for clinicians, reviewers and guideline panels to audit such claims and apply proportionate precaution.

after.title: Preprint: One algorithm, tenfold range: measurement non-equivalence makes cross-national dementia prevalence unidentifiable
after.authors: Zhu, S.; Luo, Y.
after.abstract: Background. Cross-national estimates of dementia prevalence rest on brief cognitive batteries scored against fixed cut-offs. Neither whether they measure the same construct everywhere nor how much of any cross-national difference is measurement has been formally quantified. Methods. In 66,890 adults aged [≥]65 from four population-based cohorts (USA 2016, England 2021-2023, 19 European countries 2021, China 2018) we applied a single harmonised algorithm (Langa-Weir, 27 points) and quantified how far the resulting prevalence moved across 1,152 specifications, measurement-invariance and equating models, latent class analysis, bias correction against a US gold standard, mortality and burden-of-disease anchoring, and multiple imputation. Results. Weighted prevalence ranged from 1.25% (95% CI 0.82-1.83) in England to 12.79% (11.69-13.96) in China (10.2-fold; China minus USA 7.43 points, 6.22-8.65), but the median across specifications was 2.3-fold (IQR 1.5-4.4), the 10.2-fold value sitting at the 94.6th percentile. Scalar invariance was rejected ({Delta}CFI -0.066 vs metric), driven by serial-7 subtraction (odds ratios 2.9-3.4). No operating characteristics can reproduce both the US gold standard (10.0%) and the Chinese national estimate (6.0%): the identity implies Se+Sp-1 = -1.86, outside the admissible range, which would require Chinese prevalence of at least 23.9%. A published harmonised-protocol algorithm applied to the English HCAP subsample gave 7.1% (5.7-8.7), 5.7 times the brief-algorithm value in the same population; harmonised-protocol estimates span 1.4-fold rather than 4.3-fold. Conclusions. Absolute cross-national dementia prevalence is not identifiable from brief screening algorithms. Rank order is more stable than level but is itself specification-dependent (China highest in 45%, England lowest in 65%), whereas the relative risk attached to the label is similar across cohorts (pooled mortality hazard ratio 2.14, I{superscript 2} = 0). We propose a seven-item minimum reporting standard, three items of which can be adopted immediately, and show that metric choice moves the global case count tenfold.

after.title: Preprint: Regional brain-age gaps reveal a shared polygenic architecture and regionally patterned clinical and cell-type associations
after.authors: Hwang, Y.; Park, K.-I.; Lee, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Graduate School of Data Science, Seoul National University
after.abstract: A single brain-age estimate may obscure regional differences in clinical vulnerability. Using voxel-level deep learning, we derived whole-brain and nine regional brain-age gaps (BAGs) spanning cortical, subcortical and cerebellar regions from T1-weighted MRI in 46,254 UK Biobank participants. Genetic correlation estimates in 41,067 participants (rg = 0.56-0.93) exceeded phenotypic correlations across all 45 pairs, yet regional profiles varied across 24 hospital-recorded diagnoses. Oligodendrocyte annotations predominated for whole-brain and cerebellar BAGs, whereas annotations for caudate BAG included astrocyte and vascular classes. In the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, temporal BAG showed stronger associations with cerebrospinal fluid A{beta}42 and cognition than whole-brain BAG when modelled together. A regional model modestly improved discrimination of observed conversion from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease during available follow-up compared with a whole-brain model. Polygenic scores showed cross-cohort associations with hypertension and osteoporosis. Regional BAGs provide complementary clinical information within a shared polygenic architecture.

after.title: Preprint: Continually pretrained open-weight language models can outperform traditional machine learning in EHR-based clinical prediction
after.authors: Zhou, J.; Zhang, X.; Yan, C.; Ye, J. Z.; Patel, M. B.; Novak, L. L.; Kho, A. N.; Wright, A.; Malin, B. A.; Chen, Y.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Biomedical Informatics, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, Nashville, TN, USA
after.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) prompted with electronic health record (EHR) data have predicted clinical outcomes less accurately than locally trained machine-learning models. We developed VEX-EHR by extending the vocabulary of a 12-billion-parameter open-weight LLM (weights publicly available) with 17,601 clinical and audit-log codes from 170,483 patients' records at one academic medical center, continuing its pretraining on those 2019-2024 records (4.7 billion tokens) and fine-tuning it per task. AUROCs were 0.917 for next-24-hour discharge, 0.715 for 30-day readmission and 0.847 for intensive care unit acute kidney injury, against 0.868, 0.677 and 0.828 for gradient-boosted trees and 0.848, 0.650 and 0.791 for CEHR-BERT, an EHR foundation model. Continued pretraining added 0.031-0.053 AUROC on every task. With 10% of the labels, VEX-EHR exceeded both comparators using all labels for discharge, and CEHR-BERT for readmission, valuable where labels are costly. Adapted by continued pretraining, open-weight LLMs can outperform traditional machine learning in EHR-based prediction.

after.title: Preprint: STREAM: Sequential Transformer for Risk Estimation from Asynchronous Medical Events for Dynamic Postoperative AKI Prediction
after.authors: Lu, S.; Ruan, X.; Wang, L.; Ahn, J.; Liang, Y.; Wang, X.; Wen, A.; Jiang, J.; Hu, Y.; Li, X.; Liu, H.
after.abstract: Postoperative acute kidney injury (PO-AKI) risk estimates evolve as clinical information accumulates, yet many electronic health record (EHR) models use static or fixed-window representations. We developed STREAM, a perioperative event-stream Transformer that represents irregular EHR data as chronological clinical events and supports surgery-index prediction at surgery completion and event-by-event postoperative AKI prediction. In a retrospective cohort of 167,078 noncardiac surgical episodes, STREAM achieved surgery-index AUROC/AUPRC of 0.942/0.771, the Time-series Transformer 0.933/0.729, and GRU-D 0.926/0.695. Postoperative macro-AUPRC across 6-hour evaluation intervals was 0.589, 0.525, and 0.547, respectively. STREAM showed more consistent calibration across postoperative time points than the comparators. Event-arrival attribution and within-window permutation analysis enabled event-level interpretation of how newly arrived information and fine-grained event ordering shaped evolving risk estimates. These findings support event-stream modeling as an interpretable framework for dynamic, temporally resolved prediction from longitudinal EHR data as well as a potential risk-estimation component for future perioperative digital twins.

after.title: Preprint: Transportability of polysomnography-derived sleep physiological fingerprints across cohorts, measurement modalities and time: a four-axis evaluation in four cohorts
after.authors: Deng, Q.; Chen, Y.; Ma, N.; Lou, X.
after.abstract: Epidemiological evidence linking sleep to Alzheimer disease (AD) relies predominantly on self-reported sleep, whereas cohorts with polysomnography (PSG) and cohorts with AD biomarkers rarely share participants. Multifractal long-range-interdependency representations classify obstructive sleep apnoea severity accurately across cohorts, but whether such a physiological fingerprint can be transported between cohorts, between measurement modalities or over time has not been evaluated. We propose four axes of transportability and test them in the Sleep Heart Health Study (n = 5,614), MESA Sleep (n = 2,012), ADNI (n = 2,286) and MrOS Sleep (2,911 men; 1,026 re-examined after 6.37 years; 3,928 scored nights). Axis A1, cross-cohort construct convergence, passed: PSG-derived Sleep Coupling Disruption Index loadings agreed between SHHS and MESA (cosine 0.986; Wasserstein distance 0.0487). Axis A2, incremental validity beyond the apnoea-hypopnoea index, failed: the fully adjusted hazard ratio for incident cardiovascular disease was 1.009 (95% CI 0.941-1.085; p = 0.83) and the C-index was 0.8079 with or without the index; in MrOS, adding a multifractal coupling fingerprint increased R-squared by 0.00058 (likelihood-ratio p = 0.399). Axis A3, proxy identifiability, failed: the reliability ratio linking portable subjective complaints to objective physiological burden was 1.95 x 10-5, with a bootstrap 95% upper bound of 0.00261 and 0.0027 for a semantically optimised proxy, far below the 0.25 floor required for measurement-error correction. Under classical error this implies a 370-fold sample-size inflation; Monte-Carlo power at n = 10,000 was 0.177. A nominally significant association between night-time behaviour and dementia severity would require an implausible true physiological effect of 28.7 standard deviations, and it reversed to -0.0554 after adjustment for total neuropsychiatric burden. The prespecified ADNI primary outcome, plasma pTau217, was null (beta = 0.0033, p = 0.911), as were the MrOS six-year cognitive complaint outcome (beta = -0.0204, p = 0.375) and a 35-event self-reported dementia endpoint (OR = 0.921, p = 0.679). Axis A4, temporal stability, failed: six-year test-retest reliability was r = 0.157 (95% CI 0.096-0.216) for the fingerprint versus r = 0.455 (0.405-0.502) for AHI, despite stable concurrent validity (rho = 0.380 and 0.328 with same-night AHI). Spearman-Brown projection indicates that approximately nine nights must be averaged for the fingerprint to reach a reliability of 0.60, compared with two for AHI. A fingerprint can therefore be reproducible without being transportable. We provide a four-question decision workflow and an eight-item minimum reporting set; subjective sleep complaints should not be substituted for objective sleep physiology in aetiological inference.

after.title: Preprint: Improving epidemic nowcasting with auxiliary information and geographic networks
after.authors: Lyu, R.; Turcan, A.; Wilder, B.
after.abstract: Monitoring infectious disease trends requires timely information on disease activity, but direct measurements suffer reporting delays, hindering public health response. Numerous less-direct measurements are collected rapidly, although their relationship to disease can change with behavior, reporting, and data availability. Here, we present GLCast, a statistical nowcasting framework that effectively uses auxiliary information to estimate delayed surveillance measurements, without requiring any verification beforehand that these data will improve performance. At each retraining window, GLCast automatically selects useful data streams through adaptive local regression and further learns dynamic epidemic neighbor graphs to aggregate models across. We evaluate GLCast on six years of weekly influenza-like illness with retail sales, three years of daily COVID-19 hospital admissions with search and survey signals, and seven recent influenza, COVID-19, and RSV surveillance targets with environmental, travel and online-attention streams. Against methods without auxiliary information, GLCast lowers mean prediction error by 25.1% for historical influenza-like illness and 12.9% for historical COVID-19 admissions against the strongest baselines, improving 45 of 45 and 49 of 51 evaluated jurisdictions, respectively, with further performance gains in critical upswing periods. In the seven modern targets, GLCast achieves the lowest overall error and maintains strong performance when multiple diseases experience overlapping upswings. Interpreting how GLCast uses additional information, we find that the features and neighbors selected are indeed dynamic over time and heterogeneous across different states. Interestingly, outbreaks appear to be change points where both feature and neighbor importance will dramatically shift. GLCast tends to assign new importance to auxiliary information at the peak of an outbreak, disregards neighbors during outbreaks, and heavily relies on neighbors during down periods.

after.title: Preprint: Scalable cell-state-resolved TWAS identified dynamic autoimmune disease genes along functional programs
after.authors: Yu, S.; Chen, J.; Sakaue, S.; Sun, W.; Lila, E.; Qi, G.
after.abstract: Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) are widely used to prioritize genes for complex diseases. TWAS typically trains models on expression quantitative disease locus (eQTL) reference data to predict gene expression from genotype, then tests for association between the predicted expression and disease. With the rapid growth of single-cell eQTL data, there is a pressing need for methods that can fully leverage cell-level information. We previously developed TWiST, the first method for TWAS at cell-state resolution. TWiST is powerful, but training its prediction model is computationally expensive. Here we propose Fast-TWiST, an accelerated and scalable version of TWiST that can analyze hundreds of thousands to millions of cells. Fast-TWiST computes donor-level summary statistics that retain all the information needed to fit the cell-level model, so numerical optimization runs over donors rather than individual cells. In simulations and real-data evaluations, Fast-TWiST was more than 10 times faster than TWiST while matching its statistical performance. Applying the method to the OneK1K data, we identified 3,092 dynamic gene-disease associations that depend on biologically interpretable gene programs, including cytotoxicity, immediate early gene (IEG), BCL2/FAM13A, T helper 1-like (Th1-Like), and resting T helper 2 (Th2-Resting). Independent eQTL datasets and single-cell multiome data supported cell-state-specific regulatory effects that may be driving these findings.

In this study, we compare the genetic architecture of four cohorts comprising 87 sporadic EOAD cases, 1,018 late-onset AD (LOAD) cases, 585 non-demented controls (TGEN2-AD and TGEN2-ND cohorts), and 3,487 non-demented controls from the AD Sequencing Project (ADSP-CTL). We observed a significant enrichment of the APOE epsilon 4 allele in the EOAD cohort compared to controls (52.2% vs 20.1%; p = 1.54e-10), although its frequency was lower than in the LOAD cohort (64.5%; p = 0.0298). As expected, APOE epsilon 4 was strongly enriched in the LOAD group relative to controls (p = 1.23e-63). Sporadic EOAD genome-wide association study (GWAS) analysis and sequence kernel association tests (SKAT) confirmed strong association signals in the APOE locus, including the genes APOE, APOC1, NECTIN2, and TOMM40. AD-related polygenic risk score (PRS) analysis showed that EOAD patients carried an intermediate genetic risk (mean PRS = 40.1), significantly lower than LOAD (mean PRS = 57.5; p = 6.7e-05) but higher than controls (mean PRS = 25.1; p = 6.1e-04). Notably, rare variants in autosomal dominant AD genes (APP, PSEN1, PSEN2) and previously reported EOAD/LOAD modifier genes were not enriched in the sporadic EOAD cohort. These results suggest that, despite earlier onset, sporadic EOAD is not driven by a higher polygenic burden or rare high-impact variants. Instead, its genetic architecture appears to overlap more closely with LOAD, supporting the hypothesis that EOAD may represent an early and more severe manifestation of LOAD or a genetically distinct subtype. Unidentified risk factors, such as epigenetic modifications or complex structural variants, may contribute to EOAD genetic risk and warrant further investigation to better elucidate the complex genetic architecture of Alzheimer's disease.

after.title: Preprint: rendehR: a cohort-first, provenance-aware, agentic-ready pipeline for harmonizing multi-source electronic health records
after.authors: Mussavi Rizi, M.; Shein, V.; Torres-Espin, A.
after.abstract: Objective: Public electronic health record (EHR) databases differ in schema, identifiers, coding systems, units, and event structure, making disease-specific studies across multiple sources difficult to construct and audit. We developed rendehR, a computational pipeline and R package for cohort-centered extraction and harmonization of multi-source EHR data. Materials and Methods: rendehR treats cohort definition as an explicit executable component of dataset construction. Cohorts can be defined using diagnosis codes, identifiers, R callbacks, or source-specific SQL. After cohort selection, linked source tables are restricted to the selected population and can be retained as cohort-specific Parquet datasets or loaded into a persistent database. Clinical concepts are defined using source-aware mappings, generated, or curated SQL and are harmonized into flat, time-series, and duration representations. Configuration, executable SQL, cohort metadata, concept-origin metadata, and source-level values are retained to support inspection and traceability. In the current version rendehR provides interactive R assistant wizards for workflow configuration, a Shiny application for patient-level data visualization, three agent skills for AI-assisted workflow execution and extension, and an MCP server exposing nine read-only tools for AI-assisted configuration, concept discovery, and cohort exploration. The current implementation supports MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU-CRD. We demonstrate rendehR on a reference cohort of spinal cord injury and disease (SCID). Results: Using the reference cohort, rendehR identified 4,320, 39,850, and 2,343 qualifying hospital admissions in MIMIC-III, MIMIC-IV, and eICU-CRD, respectively. Patient-level extraction expanded these cohorts to 5,725, 104,988, and 2,823 hospital admissions, with 5,983, 17,405, and 3,441 associated ICU stays, respectively. Applying the more complex Sepsis-3 case identification, rendehR identified and extracted 34,460, 41,296, and 47,035 qualifying ICU stays across the same databases, respectively. The current concept library includes 22 flat, 123 time-series, and 75 duration harmonized concepts. Conclusion: rendehR provides a cohort-centered framework for constructing disease-specific datasets from multiple heterogeneous HER sources while preserving the source-specific logic used to define cohorts and clinical concepts. The package supports reusable cohort artifacts, inspectable SQL-based concept construction, harmonized analytical representations, and traceable study-specific data pipelines.
