after.title: Preprint: Co-occurrence Is Not Evidence: Separating Protein-Disease Findings from Incidental Mentions in HFpEF Literature
after.authors: Azat, A.; De Santana Junior, C. J.; Cadeiras, M.; Liem, D. A.
after.abstract: Literature-mining pipelines such as CaseOLAP rank proteins by how often they appear next to a disease term. Appearing next to a disease is not the same as being implicated in it: in our 300-sentence held-out set of PubMed sentences that mention a protein and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), only 115 assert a biological association. The rest report a negative finding or mention the protein in passing, for example as a drug the patients were taking. We train a sentence-level filter that sorts each protein mention into associated, not_associated or incidental. It is a fine-tuned PubMedBERT trained with class-weighted cross-entropy and R-Drop regularization, combined into a six-model majority-vote ensemble over three random seeds. On the held-out set, with no thresholds tuned on it, the ensemble reaches 85.3% accuracy and 86.1% macro F1 (bootstrap 95% confidence intervals 81.0-89.3% and 82.1-89.7%), against 38.3% accuracy for the co-occurrence baseline, which counts every mention as an association. Single models average 84.4 +/- 0.7% accuracy across seeds. Run after CaseOLAP, the filter removes protein mentions that are not evidence of association from the HFpEF candidate list. Where the ensemble's majority vote disagreed with the annotation, the annotation was often wrong. Expert review of those sentences corrected 53 of 88 flagged evaluation labels and 109 training labels. Most of the errors came from one flaw in the annotation sheet: in sentences naming several proteins, it did not say which protein the label was for. The audit stage coincided with the largest accuracy gain in the project, but the same stage also changed the evaluation labels and the training loss, so we report it as a chronology, not as a controlled result.

after.abstract: Background: Preconception administration of Plasmodium falciparum sporozoite (PfSPZ) Vaccine is safe and prevents malaria during pregnancies identified within 21 months post-vaccination. We evaluated pre-conception PfSPZ Vaccine effects on malaria risk in offspring during the first year of life. Methods: In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Ouelessebougou, Mali, 300 healthy 18-38-year-old women were allocated 1:1:1 to receive 9x10^5 PfSPZ or 1.8x10^6 PfSPZ of PfSPZ Vaccine or normal saline on days 1-8-29, and followed up to 21 months for malaria endpoints and pregnancies. 104 infants from 103 pregnancies identified first year post-vaccination [9x10^5 PfSPZ (n=38); 1.8x10^6 PfSPZ (n=40); normal saline (n=26)] were seen every two months and during illnesses. Primary endpoints were blood-smear parasitemia and clinical malaria. Safety outcomes included newborn baseline characteristics and infant adverse events (AEs). Findings: Newborn baseline characteristics and infant AEs did not differ between arms; AEs were common but predominantly mild (91.9-96% Grade 1). Vaccine efficacy of 9x10^5 PfSPZ was 75.1% (95% CI 20.6-92.2) against parasitemia (10.5% parasitemic infants versus 38.5% of placebo) and 94.2% (54.9-99.3) against clinical malaria (2.6% malarious infants versus 38.5% of placebo). VE of 1.8x10^6 PfSPZ group was 40.3% (-43.6-75.2) against parasitemia and 36.3% (-50.3-73.0) against clinical malaria, both non-significant. At 6 and 12 months of age, PfCSP antibodies were similar in offspring of vaccinated and control mothers. Interpretation: Pre-conception PfSPZ Vaccine was safe and reduced Pf infection and clinical malaria during infancy in 9x10^5 PfSPZ group. Further development of preconception PfSPZ vaccines is warranted to protect mother-infant dyads.

after.authors: Souffou, M.; Demey, E.; Dambrun, M.; Emmanuel, A.; Kammoun, Z.; Dechavanne, S.; Sare, N.; Dechavanne, C.; Migot-Nabias, F.; Vinh, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Ecole Superieure de Physique et de Chimie Industrielles de la Ville de Paris
after.abstract: Objectives: Toxoplasmosis represents a significant global health burden, particularly among immunocompromised patients and newborns of mothers who contracted a primary infection during pregnancy. In the newborn, maternally transferred Toxoplasma gondii-specific IgG persist for up to six months and mask the IgG newly synthesized by the infant, delaying diagnosis. Individual polymor-phisms of the IgG heavy chain constant region (IGHG) can distinguish the two origins, but have so far been characterized only in total circulating IgG. We assessed whether this discrimination can be achieved on the IgG fraction directed against the parasite itself. Methods: Recombinant T. gondii antigens (TgSAG1, TgGRA7, TgAMA1) were produced and evaluated by ELISA on 85 seropositive and 95 seronegative plasma samples. Parasite-specific IgG were then immunopurified from a mixture of plasma from two donors, one seropositive and one seronegative, carrying distinct IGHG1 and IGHG3 alleles known from DNA sequencing, and their Fc/2 fragments were analyzed by middle-down and bottom-up LC-MS/MS. Results: TgSAG1 proved the most effective antigen; combined with TgAMA1 and/or TgGRA7 it reached 100% sensitivity and 97% specificity. Middle-down analysis offered high specificity but insufficient sensitivity for the microliter plasma volumes required in newborns. Bottom-up analysis identified the peptide WQQGNVFSCSVMHEGLHNHYTQK, characteristic of IGHG1*07, exclusively in the seropositive donor, in agreement with DNA sequencing data. Conclusion: Combining antigen-affinity immunopurification with IGHG proteotyping allows an individual IGHG allele to be assigned within a pathogen-specific polyclonal IgG fraction representing less than 0.5% of total plasma IgG. This first demonstration, obtained in a two-donor context, opens the way to distinguishing maternal from fetal specific IgG for the early diagnosis of congenital toxoplasmosis.

after.title: Preprint: Modelling the impact of a school-based influenza vaccination programme under uncertainty in seasonal transmission dynamics
after.authors: Boksenbojm, E.; Eales, O.; Cheng, A. C.; McCaw, J.; Shearer, F. M.
after.abstract: School-aged children are thought to be an important driver of influenza transmission. In this paper we study the direct and indirect health effects of a school-based live-attenuated influenza vaccination (LAIV) programme in Australia, using a stochastic, age-stratified model of seasonal influenza transmission. The model was calibrated using Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) in order to capture uncertainty in influenza infection dynamics. The calibrated model was used to evaluate programmes varying in target age group, vaccination coverage and vaccine effectiveness. On average, school-based LAIV programmes reduced infections and hospitalisations at the population level across all scenarios, with greater reductions at higher coverage and vaccine effectiveness and when both primary- and secondary-school-aged children were targeted. However, estimated effects varied substantially across plausible transmission dynamics, particularly indirect effects --- for some programme scenarios, we estimated that in non-target age groups both near complete suppression or a small increase in infections were possible outcomes. For all scenarios, we estimated that school-based LAIV programmes would lead to a reduction in infections and hospitalisations in target age groups.

after.authors: Mihretu, A.; Dereb, M.
after.abstract: Background Injuries and violence disproportionately affect disadvantaged populations, particularly males, young people and those living in low- and middle-income countries, where about 90% of injury-related deaths occur. Preventing injuries is integral to achieving several Sustainable Development Goals. This study aimed to assess the magnitude, characteristics, spatial distribution, and individual- and household-level determinants of intentional injuries in Ethiopia. Methods We analysed the 2024-25 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey, a two-stage stratified cluster survey of 21,241 households (97,262 members) in 797 geo-referenced clusters. Household respondents reported injuries among members in the preceding 12 months; injuries due to violence/assault, self-harm or conflict were classified as intentional. Survey-weighted rates per 100,000 were estimated. Spatial patterns were assessed with global Moran's I, Getis-Ord Gi* hotspot analysis and Kulldorff's Poisson scan statistic. Survey-weighted logistic regression compared intentional with unintentional non-traffic injuries (n = 222), and survey-weighted Poisson regression estimated household-level incidence rate ratios (IRRs). after.abstract: BACKGROUND: Auditory oddball responses, including the mismatch negativity (MMN), are impaired in patients with schizophrenia (SZ) and bipolar disorder (BP). Biophysical modelling of cortical microcircuit function and effective connectivity implicates reduced synaptic gain of excitatory pyramidal cells in patients with SZ, but whether similar alterations are present in adolescents with familial or genetic risk remains unknown. METHODS: We studied 15-year-old adolescents enrolled in The Danish High Risk and Resilience Study, VIA 15. We measured auditory oddball responses in 59 adolescents at familial high risk for SZ (FHR-SZ), 38 adolescents at familial high risk for BP (FHR-BP), and 75 population-based controls (PBC) using magnetoencephalography (MEG) during a roving oddball paradigm. We investigated sensor- and source-level evoked responses and modelled effective connectivity using dynamic causal modelling (DCM). We examined the impact of familial and polygenic risk for SZ and BP, and associations with global level of functioning and auditory psychotic experiences. RESULTS: Sensor- and source-level analyses did not detect statistically significant differences in oddball responses between adolescents at FHR-SZ and FHR-BP compared with PBC. However, DCM analyses revealed reduced oddball-dependent gain of pyramidal cells in an empirically determined left frontal source in FHR-SZ and FHR-BP adolescents compared with PBC, and this was associated with lower levels of functioning across groups. CONCLUSIONS: Biophysical modelling of auditory oddball responses identifies surprise-related differences in effective connectivity in adolescents at FHR-SZ and FHR-BP. These findings suggest that microcircuit dysregulation, particularly in frontal synaptic gain, may serve as an early marker of vulnerability.

after.authors: Tsai, S.; Iveson, M.; Klose, D.; Milaneschi, Y.; Penninx, B. W. J. H.; Kwong, A. S. F.; Whalley, H. C.; Bullmore, E. T.; Khandaker, G. M.; McIntosh, A. M.; Shen, X.
after.abstract: Antidepressants are widely prescribed, yet their biological mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Large-scale metabolomics and linked electronic health records provide a unique opportunity to characterise metabolic profiles associated with medication exposure. We investigated metabolic signatures of antidepressant exposure using 251 nuclear magnetic resonance biomarkers in UK Biobank (N = 222,911), with external validation in NESDA and ALSPAC (N = 6,082) and longitudinal analyses (n = 5,820, mean follow-up = 4.2 years). We identified 152 metabolites associated with current antidepressant use (PFDR < 0.05), characterised by elevated triglycerides and very-low-density lipoproteins. Current users also showed higher omega-3 fatty acid levels and lower omega-6-to-omega-3 ratios, both associated with lower depression risk. Metabolic profile scores significantly distinguished antidepressant users in both external cohorts (OR = 1.07-1.39, ROC AUC = 0.58-0.73). Longitudinal analyses identified nominal associations between antidepressant initiation and increases in nine lipid biomarkers (effect size = 0.144-0.229). These findings suggest metabolic signatures associated with antidepressant use may not be solely explained by underlying depression and are characterised by both potentially beneficial fatty acid alterations and adverse lipid profiles. Validation across independent cohorts and consistency with longitudinal findings strengthen our evidence, supporting insights into antidepressant mechanism and its relevance to cardiometabolic health.

after.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a critical global health threat exacerbated by inappropriate antibiotic use, yet evidence on caregivers' awareness and practices in Bangladesh remains limited. This cross-sectional study assessed AMR awareness, antibiotic use practices, and information sources among 225 caregivers using a structured questionnaire that also captured socio-demographic characteristics. Understanding of AMR was poor: although 78% recognized that antibiotics are effective against bacterial infections, only 35% acknowledged that they are ineffective against viral infections. Regarding practices, 30% discontinued antibiotic courses prematurely and 40% reported self-medication, primarily guided by pharmacy advice (45%) or previous prescriptions (30%). Healthcare professionals were the leading source of information (55%), followed by media (30%) and community programs (15%). Knowledge differed significantly across socio-demographic groups, with higher awareness among caregivers who were more educated, urban-dwelling, and from wealthier households (p<0.05). These findings reveal a substantial gap between AMR knowledge and antibiotic practices, particularly regarding misuse for viral infections, premature cessation, and self-medication. Targeted educational interventions, stronger enforcement of prescription regulations, and improved healthcare access are urgently needed, and behavioral interventions should address both knowledge deficits and practical barriers to help curb AMR in Bangladesh.

after.authors: Ellis, B.; Jestico, E.; Treloar, D.; McAuslan, N.; Careless, H.; Davies, E.; Bould, H.; Kidger, J.; Warne, N.
after.abstract: Background: School prevention strategies are key to reducing the impact of youth mental health difficulties, such as depression and anxiety. Visual art programmes may be beneficial for prevention but evidence is limited. To better understand the potential for visual arts-based prevention programmes in schools, we explored staff experiences of using visual art for mental health and views on what is needed to facilitate successful programmes. Methods: We used a convergent mixed-methods approach, combining online surveys (n=77) and in-depth interviews (n=27) from art teachers and staff supporting student mental health in UK secondary schools. Complementary survey and interview questions covered current use of visual art for student mental health, what a visual art prevention programme might look like, and potential concerns. We conducted descriptive statistics for quantitative survey data and reflexive thematic analysis for qualitative survey and interview data. Results: Visual arts were seen as important for student mental health and commonly used: 65.8% of staff used visual arts to support student mental health in the last year, and 31.6% did so weekly, despite most participants reporting no relevant training. Theme 1,  Art is a sanctuary in the school day, considered art as intrinsically linked to mental health, with art freedom conferring particular benefits. Theme 2,  Resources in schools are stretched, represented the pressure of school environments, limited resources and need for prevention. Theme 3,  Integration, flexibility and relationships as factors for success, highlighted integrating programmes into school practice, enabling flexibility and choice, and building positive relationships between students, school staff and external providers are key for success. Conclusions: Despite implementation challenges, visual arts-based prevention approaches were viewed positively. We recommend school mental health arts programmes should promote school ownership, include creative freedom, be flexible to schools and students needs, and be supported by both internal school staff and external providers.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health
after.abstract: Importance: While recent changes in federal vaccine policy may have negatively impacted clinician vaccination efforts, data assessing such impacts are limited. Objective: To evaluate the impact on clinicians of these changes to vaccine recommendations. Design: A high-quality panel survey was administered in July 2026 and compared to a similar survey administered in January 2023. Setting: The panel consisted of clinicians from across the United States. Participants: Respondents included 508 pediatricians, 500 family physicians, 166 nurse practitioners (NPs), 167 physician assistants (PAs), and 166 nurses. Main Outcomes and Measures: Primary outcomes of interest included clinician strength of vaccine recommendations for patients and trusted sources of vaccine information and recommendations. Results: Most clinicians trusted vaccine recommendations from professional medical organizations such as the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) (91%) and the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) (90%), whereas fewer than half of clinicians trusted vaccine recommendations from federal agencies such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) (47%) or the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) (42%). Compared to 2023, far fewer clinicians reported trusting vaccine information from CDC (47% vs 79%) or FDA (43% vs 75%) (adjusted p<0.01). Despite reduced trust in federal vaccine recommendations, most clinicians continued to recommend routine vaccines for their patients, with the notable exception of COVID-19, for which far fewer clinicians recommend vaccination compared to 2023 regardless of patient age, but especially among 12-15-year-olds (41% vs 71%, p<0.01) and 16-24-year-olds (43% vs 74%, p<0.01). Many clinicians also reported noticing substantial increases in the frequency (80%) and intensity (76%) of patient vaccine concerns over the past year, as well as in their time spent discussing vaccines with patients (61%) and looking up vaccine information (45%). Conclusions and Relevance: This survey provides insight into the point-of-care impact of recent changes in federal vaccine policy and the shifts in clinician vaccine recommendations and trusted sources of vaccine information since the end of the pandemic. Professional associations can fill the current void in federal leadership by providing clinicians with reliable vaccine information and recommendations.

after.title: Preprint: The relationship between vaccination and preventive measures in case of infection and hospitalization: a cross-sectional study of Algeria using a Bayesian approach
after.authors: ahmed, h.
after.abstract: Response variables, in the form of categorical variables with numerous predictors, are often modeled using logistic regression models. A regression coefficient expresses the contribution of a predictor variable to the response variable through the parameter beta. Therefore, estimating the regression coefficient beta is necessary. The Bayesian approach is used to estimate regression coefficients in this research. The Bayesian technique combines information from sample data with prior knowledge of the characteristics of the parameters of interest to provide updated, or posterior, information. In this work, attention focuses on the COVID-19 epidemic in Algeria. We study the association between COVID-19 preventive measures and the risk of infection and hospitalization. Through this approach, we examine the role of preventive measures among vaccinated and unvaccinated individuals in relation to the risk of infection and hospitalization. This study determined that the association between barrier measures and infection among unvaccinated individuals was not statistically significant (odds ratio [OR] = 0.77359; 95% credible interval [CrI] = 0.55-1.05). On the other hand, barrier measures were strongly associated with infection among vaccinated individuals. An odds ratio of 0.11 indicates that vaccinated individuals who did not apply barrier measures had approximately nine times the odds of infection compared with vaccinated individuals who applied these measures. Individuals who did not apply barrier measures and were not vaccinated had approximately 4.65 times the odds of hospitalization compared with individuals who applied barrier measures but were not vaccinated (OR = 0.215; 95% CrI = 0.06-0.47). Among vaccinated individuals, those who did not apply barrier measures had 1.87 times the estimated odds of hospitalization compared with those who applied these measures (OR = 1.87; 95% CrI = 0.27-7.29). However, this association was not statistically significant because the credible interval included 1. According to this study, older individuals are more vulnerable when preventive measures are not strictly followed. Vaccination is also an important factor associated with reduced hospitalization, particularly among older individuals.

after.abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a time-sensitive medical emergency in which rapid recognition of right ventricular (RV) dysfunction by point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) can support early risk stratification. Here, we present HOPE (ecHO-Pulmonary Embolism), a real-world emergency cardiac POCUS video dataset comprising 4,069 patients with suspected PE, and EchoPE, a foundation-model-based video classification framework for detecting PE-associated right-heart phenotypes. HOPE includes five commonly acquired emergency echocardiographic views, with all positive PE cases confirmed by computed tomography pulmonary angiography. EchoPE builds on EchoPrime-pretrained echocardiographic representations and incorporates view recognition, task-specific adaptation, and attention-based interpretability. Experiments suggested that directly transferring EchoPrime representations to this disease-specific task provided limited performance, whereas EchoPE (AUROC 95.2 +/- 0.3) substantially outperformed both EchoPrime with a classification head (AUROC 87.6 +/- 1) and conventional video deep learning baselines. At a fixed sensitivity of 90%, EchoPE achieved a precision of 87.8, compared with 70.7 for EchoPrime. Among adaptation strategies, Low-Rank Adaptation combined with knowledge distillation provided the best balance between PE discrimination and preservation of pretrained echocardiographic semantics. after.abstract: Objectives: To describe bacterial STI burden and examine its association with time-varying oral PrEP use among participants in a multinational HIV prevention efficacy trial. Methods: We conducted a post-hoc analysis of HVTN 704/HPTN 085 (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT02716675), a randomized, placebo-controlled study of the VRC01 broadly neutralizing antibody for HIV prevention. Men and transgender persons who have sex with men were enrolled in Brazil, Peru, United States, and Switzerland (April 2016-October 2018). All participants received an enhanced prevention package including STI testing every six months and optional access to oral PrEP. Prevalence and incidence of chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis were described. Cox proportional hazards models estimated associations between time-varying PrEP use and incident STIs. Results: Among 2,687 participants, 27.9% had a bacterial STI at enrollment (chlamydia 11.1%, gonorrhea 10.2%, syphilis 13.1%). Prevalence was higher in Brazil (36.7%) and Peru (34.9%) than in the United States/Switzerland (21.4%). Rectal and oropharyngeal infections predominated. Among participants negative at baseline, incidence of any bacterial STI was 29.4 per 100 person-years (95% CI: 27.2-31.7). Incidence was higher during periods of PrEP use than non-use (HR 1.75, 95% CI: 1.44-2.13), consistent across pathogens. Conclusions: In this multinational HIV prevention trial, bacterial STI burden was high, particularly in Latin America and at extragenital sites. STI incidence was higher during periods of reported oral PrEP use. These findings highlight the importance of integrating multisite STI testing, treatment, counseling, and targeted prevention into HIV prevention services and future efficacy trials.

after.abstract: Background: Dietary guidelines emphasize the consumption of plant-based protein foods for cardiovascular health. However, it remains unclear how the balance of plant- and animal-based protein food consumption contributes to muscle health. Objective: Our objective was to estimate the effect of increasing the consumption of plant- (PLANT) relative to animal-based (ANIMAL) protein foods on physical function, including muscle function, strength, and lean mass, in middle-aged and older adults. We also examined the effects of increasing both protein sources (BOTH), within a healthy dietary pattern (HEALTHY), or limiting animal protein foods consumption (HEALTHY-P+). Methods: Non-experimental data from the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA) comprehensive cohort were used to emulate a target trial. Middle-aged and older adults were followed for 6 years. Sociodemographic and diet data (frequency via the Short Diet Questionnaire) were assessed every three years. Objectively measured outcomes were muscle function (Timed Up&Go, 4-m walking speed, chair rise time), appendicular lean soft tissue (ALST) by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry and handgrip strength. The parametric g-formula was used to account for time-varying confounding and loss to follow-up. Results: A total of 21,636 participants were eligible (median [Q1-Q3] age, 62 [54-70] years; 49% female). Across all hypothetical interventions, the HEALTHY intervention consistently improved outcomes. Compared with no intervention, HEALTHY yielded the largest estimated differences: Timed Up&Go (-0.15 s; 95%CI: -0.24, -0.07), chair rise time (-0.03 s; 95%CI: -0.06, -0.01), handgrip strength (+0.5 kg; 95%CI: 0.3, 0.7), and ALST (+0.12 kg, 95%CI: 0.05-0.18). BOTH showed consistent but smaller effect estimates. Further limiting animal protein did not confer additional benefits. Interventions increasing PLANT or ANIMAL alone showed 95%CIs compatible with no effect. Effect estimate magnitudes were below clinically important differences. Conclusion: In middle-aged and older adults, findings suggest that a balanced approach to increasing consumption of both animal and plant-based protein foods may yield modest benefits for muscle health compared with no intervention, particularly within a healthy dietary pattern.

after.abstract: Background: Standardized health-related quality of life (HRQoL) measures may not capture all symptoms/problems relevant to people with cancer. The European Oncology Quality of Life toolkit (EUonQoL-Kit), co-created with multiple stakeholders to inform health policy across Europe, combines standardized closed-ended patient-reported outcome (PRO) items with the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) open-ended Write In three Symptoms/Problems (WISP) instrument. We aimed to identify symptoms/problems reported via WISP beyond the EUonQoL-Kit, examine differences in background characteristics between WISP respondents and non-respondents, and compare additional symptom/problem reporting across three target cancer populations: patients in active treatment, survivors, and patients in palliative care. Methodology: This descriptive analysis used data from adults with current or previous cancer diagnoses participating in a multicenter validation study across 32 European countries (22 August 2024 - 7 July 2025). WISP responses were categorized, and subsequently their prevalence and severity were calculated. Participant characteristics and the ten most frequently reported additional symptoms/problems were compared across groups using t-tests, chi-square tests, or Fisher's exact tests, as appropriate. Results: Among 4,284 included participants, 519 (12.1%) reported 954 symptoms/problems on WISP, of which 383 (40.1%) were not covered by EUonQoL-Kit v2 closed-ended items. Women, participants from Western and Northern Europe, highly educated and those diagnosed with breast cancer were more likely to respond to the WISP than other subgroups (all p < 0.05). No statistically significant differences were found in the prevalence of common additional symptoms/problems (p [≥] 0.130). Descriptively, numbness/tingling, skin problems and bleeding were most reported by patients in active treatment; indigestion, incontinence, and vision problems in survivors; and edema, cough and itching in palliative care. Conclusions: The EORTC WISP complemented standardized PRO assessment by capturing additional symptoms/problems. Integrating open-ended WISP reporting into the final toolkit may enhance HRQoL assessment across European cancer populations while identifying population-specific concerns without expanding predefined items for all respondents.

after.abstract: Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is an ultra-rare cancer defined by EWSR1-CREB gene family fusions with clinical outcomes that range from indolent to chemotherapy-refractory metastatic disease. Through multi-omic profiling of primary, recurrent and metastatic tumours and cell lines, we show that CCS is more genomically complex than previously recognised. Beyond the fusion, tumours acquire chromoplexy, chromothripsis and an intermediate aneuploidy burden, with ongoing subclonal diversification. Recurrent events include chromosome17q gain and inactivation of the MYC antagonist MGA. Enriched transcriptional signatures of chromosomal instability,17q gain, 9p21.3 loss and TERT alteration each double the hazard of death, supporting a new molecular based CCS risk stratification framework at diagnosis. Transcriptomes converge on a MYC-driven ribosome biogenesis programme, a previously unrecognised therapeutic vulnerability. These findings address a central paradox of CCS, a shared oncogenic identity with divergent clinical fate, implicating tolerated aneuploidy and chromosomal diversification as candidate determinants of progression.

after.title: Preprint: Does altering antiretroviral therapy impact an individual's gut microbiome?
after.authors: Lindergard, G.; Mann, E.; MacDonald, M.; Ustianowski, A.
after.abstract: Introduction. People with HIV are living with increased chronic inflammation with gut microbiome dysbiosis and microbial translocation emerging as contributing factors to inflammation and development of HIV associated co-morbidities. Single time-point cross-sectional population studies of individuals on antiretroviral drug therapy have suggested that some classes of antiretroviral therapy, ART, affect the gut microbiome more than others. There is, however, a lack of data examining the microbiome changes prospectively in individuals before and after alteration of their antiretroviral regiment. This study prospectively assesses changes in individuals bacterial gut microbiome when switching from one antiretroviral drug or delivery method to another class or delivery method. Methods. We conducted an observational prospective study of the gut microbiome in virologically controlled HIV infected individuals who were going through a planned switch of their ART regimen. We enrolled 15 participants and stool samples were collected before and 3-6 weeks after the switch of ART and analysed via shallow shotgun metagenomics. Results. We did not detect a statistically significant overall difference in microbiome perturbation between the study participant group that switched their antiretroviral therapy compared to the controls who continued with the same ART during the timeframe of the study. Though underpowered to detect changes in subgroups, a noticeable observational shift in the 20 most abundant bacterial species was seen when individuals changed from a protease inhibitor-based regime to a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor, NNRTI, based regimen. Individuals who changed from NNRTI based treatment to integrase inhibitor-based treatment and from integrase inhibitor-based ART to protease inhibitor-based ART demonstrated numerical changes and shifts that failed to meet statistical significance. The initiation of intramuscular delivery of ART and a move away from oral drug did not result in a significant shift in the bacterial community in stool samples in this limited number of individuals. Conclusion. We did not see statistically significant changes that were larger than those observed in controls in this small study. Switching from protease inhibitor to NNRTI demonstrated the largest shift in bacterial species that had been previously associated with positive health outcomes, indicating that protease inhibitor-based regimen might have a negative effect on the gut microbiome. Further larger prospective studies are planned to explore this area.

after.title: Preprint: Cross-cohort benchmarking and validation reveals task-dependent generalisability in tuberculosis blood transcriptomic classification
after.authors: Alex, B.; Patel, S. K.; Tiwari, B.
after.abstract: Whole-blood transcriptomic signatures are widely proposed for tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis, but reported performance often degrades when applied to new populations. We attempt to identify how much of this can be attributed to variables like model choice, panels, tasks and cohorts. We evaluated three trained classifiers (logistic regression, random forest and a multilayer perceptron) alongside two untrained scores (singscore and directional gene average). These were applied to four published panels: Kaforou (task-specific), Zak16, Sweeney3 and Berry86. Two panels were derived internally and benchmarked: Nat(mRMR), and Nat. They were compared with 50 size-matched random panels for control and significance testing. The analysis used 952 unique samples from 10 public GEO series across three diagnostic tasks, with rotating leave-one-cohort-out (LOCO) validation. Two independent cohorts, GSE144127 active tuberculosis (ATB) vs other disease (OD) and GSE152218 (ATB vs latent tuberculosis (LTB)), served as external validation; in these, panels were compared with Holm-adjusted paired DeLong tests. Generalisability was strongly task-dependent: ATB vs LTB achieved excellent cross-cohort generalisation, consistent with previous reports. However, for ATB vs LTB random panels performed comparably, with performance only diverging when panel sizes shrank, indicating that the task itself is simpler than the others. ATB vs OD exhibited lower performance depending on the panel chosen (AUCs of 0.40-0.94; median 0.75), with the mRMR-derived panel accounting for the lower bound and failing to exceed random panels in any fold. LTB vs control (CON) showed no discernible signal across panels, models and random controls (AUC 0.39-0.78; median 0.57). Model architecture exerted minimal influence compared to the underlying biological signal, with an exception for the ATB vs OD task. Both of the final locked panels were then tested on fully independent cohorts (AUC 0.86 and 0.96). There was no significant difference between these and the published panels post Holm adjustment. An additional test on sarcoidosis had failure across all panels.

after.authors: Wagner, W. P.; Smith, B.; Long, D. P.; Thomas, S. J.; Businelle, M.; Gamble, K. L.; Cropsey, K. L.
after.abstract: Biochemical verification of smoking outcomes is standard for determining the efficacy of treatments in smoking cessation clinical trials. The most common, cost-effective, and non-invasive biochemical verification method is breath carbon monoxide (CO) monitoring. No studies have examined the natural course of CO reduction in forced abstinence settings over multiple days with multiple devices to determine optimal cutoffs. This project compared the four most commonly used CO monitors (Vitalograph BreathCO, piCO+, iCOquit [corded and Bluetooth]) across 44 hours of monitoring on an inpatient hospital unit for 26 participants who reported daily cigarette smoking. Linear mixed models were used to fit smooth curves and control within subject correlations. Receiver operator characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed using logistic regression to examine performance of different cut-offs for CO for each device using sensitivity, specificity, Youden's J, area under the curve (AUC), and efficiency. By the end of monitoring (>40 hours), 100% of participants had a <3 ppm on Vitalograph BreathCO. Using the Vitalograph BreathCO as the gold standard, both the bluetooth and corded iCOquits had an optimal cutoff of <3 ppm, while the piCO+ had an optimal cutoff of <5 ppm. CO monitors demonstrated different cutoffs and should not be used interchangeably. Cutoffs higher than 5 ppm should not be used to indicate abstinence, regardless of CO device.

after.authors: Kahusu, C. M.; Oostvogels, S.; Michiels, J.; Dhondt, E.; Buys, M.; Tsoumanis, A.; EBO-BOOST-BRIDGE consortium,  ; Likofata, J.; Mukadi-Bamuleka, D.; Kavunga-Membo, H.; Mulangu, S.; Arien, K. K.; Adriaensen, W.
after.abstract: Background: The ongoing Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) highlights the absence of a licensed Bundibugyo virus (BDBV) vaccine. Ebola virus (EBOV) vaccines can induce cross-reactive BDBV binding antibodies, but evidence of cross-neutralizing antibodies is limited. Methods: In the EBO-BOOST trial (NCT06126822), previously EBOV-vaccinated adults received an ERVEBO booster after primary vaccination with ERVEBO (E|E, n=60) or ZABDENO/MVABEA (Zm|E, n=40). Neutralizing antibodies against EBOV and BDBV were measured at baseline, day 21 (D21) and month 6 (M6) using biologically contained EBOV-dVP30-eGFP and BDBV-dVP30-eGFP reporter viruses. Results: BDBV seropositivity increased from 8% at baseline to 67% at D21, declining to 34% at M6. Median NT50 titers were significantly lower for BDBV than for EBOV at D21 (40.9 vs 244.1; P<0.001) and at M6 (<20 vs 66.5; P<0.001). In mixed-effects models adjusted for time since primary vaccination, BDBV responses were 65% lower than EBOV responses at D21 (GMR 0.35; 95% CI 0.26-0.48) and 50% lower at M6 (GMR 0.50; 95% CI 0.40-0.63). The Zm|E group showed a higher BDBV fold change from baseline at D21 than the E|E group (GMR 1.75; p=0.023). Conclusions: An ERVEBO booster induces BDBV cross-neutralizing antibodies in most recipients, but responses are lower than against EBOV and largely wane by 6 months. Although protective significance and correlates of protection remain to be established, these findings support evaluation of ERVEBO in parallel with BDBV-specific vaccines.

after.title: Preprint: Fit-for-purpose bioanalytical validation of a three-cytokine human PBMC ELISpot panel (IFN-γ, IL-2, IL-4) using CEFX and CPI antigen pools for clinical trial immunomonitoring under a GLP-aligned quality system
after.authors: Li, K.; Tang, M.; Zhai, X.; Cao, H.; Guo, P.; Zhang, N.; Fan, P.; Jiang, L.; Cui, Z.; Wang, H.; Wang, Z.
after.author_corresponding_institution: JOINN Medical Testing Laboratories (Beijing) Co., Ltd.
after.abstract: Cellular immunity is an increasingly required endpoint in clinical trials of vaccines, immuno-oncology agents, and cell therapies. Multi-cytokine validation packages under a single quality system remain uncommon, and the permissible interval between blood draw and plating or freezing is rarely demonstrated experimentally. We performed GLP-aligned, fit-for-purpose validation of three human peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) ELISpot assays, following Global CRO Council recommendations and FDA, NMPA, and CFDI guidance. IFN-gamma and IL-2 were stimulated with CEFX Ultra SuperStim Pool (24 h each, plus a validated 48 h IFN-gamma regimen) and IL-4 with CPI Antigen Pool (CTL-CPI-001; 48 h) throughout all validation arms. We characterized limit of detection (LOD), lower limit of quantification (LLOQ), precision, linearity across six plating densities, robustness, pre-analytical PBMC functional stability under five delayed-processing conditions in fresh and cryopreserved arms. All assays met predefined criteria (>=80% of samples with %CV <=40% above LLOQ; R^2 >=0.97); LOD/LLOQ were 13/20 and 37/45 SFU/well for IFN-gamma at 24 h and 48 h, 9/27 for IL-2, and 4/27 for IL-4. Freshly plated PBMC remained within acceptance after up to 8 h plus 24 h of ambient holding, whereas cryopreservation after prolonged delay failed at 8+16 h for IL-2 and IL-4 and at 8+24 h for all three assays, driven by post-thaw viability less than 80%. These data define evidence-based sample-handling windows for multicenter trials. The resulting three-cytokine platform is fit-for-purpose for regulated clinical immunomonitoring.

after.title: Preprint: External validation of the EK-LEF electrocardiogram model for left ventricular systolic dysfunction in three U.S. health systems
after.authors: Malinkovich, J.; Leshchiner, M.; Knight, B.; Gong, J.; Sinha, T.
after.abstract: Background: Heart failure is projected to affect more than 11 million U.S. adults by 2050, and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) can be present before symptoms appear. Deep learning models can detect reduced LVEF from the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), but most have been tested only in the institutions that developed them, often after excluding patients with prior heart failure or recordings of poor quality. We evaluated EK-LEF, a self-supervised ECG model fine-tuned on low LVEF detection. Methods: A bidirectional Mamba encoder was pre-trained on 435,420 unlabeled MIMIC-IV ECGs and fine-tuned on 471,248 ECG-echocardiogram pairs from 235,969 patients at Mayo Clinic Rochester and the Mayo Clinic Health System. Mayo Clinic Florida served as the validation set and Mayo Clinic Arizona, a geographically distinct region, as the internal test set, each evaluated with one pair per patient. For external validation, Dandelion Health ran the model on one ECG from each of 17,500 patients at five hospitals in three U.S. health systems. The reference standard was LVEF [≤] 40% on transthoracic echocardiography within 15 days of the ECG. The primary outcomes were sensitivity and specificity. Results: In the Florida validation set of 14,880 patients, 9.9% of whom had LVEF [≤] 40%, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.951 (95% CI 0.947-0.955). In the Arizona internal test set of 16,298 patients (prevalence 9.2%), it was 0.955 (0.950-0.959), with a sensitivity of 85.0% (83.1-86.8) and a specificity of 91.7% (91.3-92.2). The signal-quality rule excluded 2.2% of internal test recordings and 0.9% of external ECGs. Among the 17,344 external patients, of whom 9.4% had LVEF [≤] 40%, the model reached an AUROC of 0.912 (0.906-0.919), a sensitivity of 85.7% (84.1-87.4) and a specificity of 81.8% (81.3-82.4), and its negative predictive value was 98.2% (98.0-98.5). Sensitivity ranged from 79.5% to 90.2% between hospitals, and specificity was lowest in patients with a recorded cardiomyopathy (56.1%). Conclusions: EK-LEF retained high sensitivity and specificity at hospitals outside the health system in which it was developed. A negative result may help identify patients who do not need echocardiography.

after.title: Preprint: A shared cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk marker phenotype: physiological context and prognosis
after.authors: Wu, J.; Chen, Q.; Chen, X.; Wu, M.; Mi, S.; Shin, H. J.; Song, H.-J.; Kim, D. W.; Zhou, Z.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, The First Affiliated Hospital (Southwest Hospital), Army Medical University, Chongqing, China.
after.abstract: Abnormalities in routine cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk markers often cluster. We characterised their common pattern, the shared adverse physiological axis (SAPA), using systolic and diastolic blood pressure, low- and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglycerides, glycated haemoglobin, body mass index and C-reactive protein. The pattern recurred across clinical cohorts and genetic data. The genetic direction retained an estimated 71.8-91.1% of the linear genetic information these eight markers carried for myocardial infarction and stroke. At similar total fat, participants with higher SAPA had more visceral and less leg fat. Differences in the variability and regional distribution of body fat contributed to weaker marker covariation at older ages, where anatomical associations persisted. The fixed clinical score also distinguished stroke prognosis among Chinese participants initially classified as low risk. Net stroke probabilities over approximately seven years were 2.560% (95% interval, 1.742-3.431%) and 9.351% (5.906-13.037%) in the low and high SAPA groups.

after.authors: Bel Haj Hassen, Y.; Ben Nacef, I.; Kefi, A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Faculty of Medicine of Tunis, University of Tunis El Manar
after.abstract: ackground: Glucocorticoid-induced diabetes mellitus (GIDM) is a frequent but under-documented complication of systemic corticosteroid therapy. We aimed to estimate its incidence and identify patient- and treatment-related risk factors. Methods: We conducted a retrospective, single-centre cohort study in the Department of Endocrinology and Internal Medicine A, Charles Nicolle Hospital, Tunis, between January 2000 and December 2020. Ninety-five adults without known diabetes (baseline HbA1c < 6.5%) starting corticosteroid therapy were followed for GIDM. Univariate predictors (p < 0.05) were entered into a multivariable model. Results: Mean age was 42.6 years (M/F ratio 0.79). GIDM developed in 57 of 95 patients (60%), after a median of 20 days (range 7-120); 40% of cases occurred within the first month. The median initial dose was 60 mg/day prednisone-equivalent, and 84% received high-dose therapy. On univariate analysis, older age, family history of type 2 diabetes, higher baseline fasting glucose, higher body weight, and methylprednisolone boluses were associated with GIDM; sex, body mass index and hypertension were not. After adjustment, only family history of type 2 diabetes (RR 1.75, 95% CI 1.18-2.61) and higher baseline fasting glucose (RR 1.37 per 1 mmol/L, 95% CI 1.07-1.75) remained independent predictors. Conclusion: GIDM occurred in three-fifths of patients, usually within the first month of therapy. Family history of type 2 diabetes and baseline fasting glucose independently identify patients warranting glycaemic surveillance from treatment initiation. Keywords: diabetes mellitus; glucocorticoids; corticosteroids; risk factors; cohort study.

after.title: Preprint: Meta-analysis of Sequencing Data Identifies Candidate Endometrial Cancer Susceptibility Genes
after.authors: Laker, M.; O'Mara, T. A.; Spurdle, A. B.; Tischkowitz, M.; Pharoah, P. A.; Davidson, E. J.; Easton, D.; Antoniou, A. C.; Yang, X.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Centre for Cancer Genetic Epidemiology, University of Cambridge, Cambridge, UK
after.abstract: Background: Endometrial cancer is the most common gynaecological malignancy in high-income countries, yet its genetic architecture remains incompletely understood. While pathogenic variants in mismatch repair genes are well-established contributors, the role of rare variants in other genes has not been systematically characterized. Methods: We evaluated associations between rare genetic variants and endometrial cancer risk based on 2,675 cases and 160,654 controls from the UK Biobank and the 100,000 Genomes Project. Gene-level associations were assessed using burden tests, with protein-truncating variants (PTVs) and missense variants (MSVs) predicted to be deleterious analysed separately. Results: Endometrial cancer (EC) risk associations were observed for three established EC susceptibility genes in the rare PTV analysis: MSH6 (RR = 36.6, 95% CI 25.9-51.8), MLH1 (RR = 52.5, 95% CI 21.3-129.4) and MSH2 (RR = 13.0, 95% CI 6.0-28.2). In the rare MSV analysis, PTEN was also significantly associated with EC risk (RR = 9.7, 95% CI 4.0-23.7). Beyond these established susceptibility genes, exome-wide significance was observed for 19 additional genes in the PTV analysis, including PHKG2 (RR = 29.8, 95% CI 9.6-92.8), and eight additional genes in the MSV analysis. Conclusion: This study identifies novel candidate genes associated with endometrial cancer risk, providing a foundation for future replication studies.

after.title: Preprint: Productivity-adjusted life years lost due to type 2 diabetes by socioeconomic position in Germany between 2022 and 2060
after.authors: Piedboeuf-Potyka, K.; Hering, R.; Schulz, M.; Brinks, R.; Hoyer, A.; Wirth, M.; Toennies, T.
after.abstract: Introduction: Type 2 diabetes can impair productivity during working age (20-69 years), causing substantial economic burden at individual and at population level. We aimed to estimate age- and sex-specific productivity-adjusted life years (PALYs) lost due to type 2 diabetes by socioeconomic position (SEP) between 2022 and 2060 in Germany. Methods: We used an established projection model and nationally representative, publicly available German data to estimate age- and sex-specific PALYs lost due to type 2 diabetes by SEP among working-age adults, accounting for future incidence trends. PALYs lost were calculated as the sum of years of life lost (YLL) and years of productivity lost (YPL) due to reduced labour force participation, presenteeism, and absenteeism, using SEP-specific estimates from representative studies. Results: Productivity losses were highest among persons with low SEP, followed by those with medium and high SEP. In 2022, 20-year-old men with type 2 diabetes and low, medium, and high SEP were projected to lose 11.32 PALYs (95% confidence interval (CI) 7.99-14.56), 8.19 PALYs (95% CI 6.01-10.33), and 3.78 PALYs (95% CI 0.89-6.72), respectively, by age 69 compared with men without type 2 diabetes, mainly driven by YPL. A comparable socioeconomic gradient was observed among women and remained largely unchanged until 2060. At the population level, an estimated 9.5 million PALYs (95% CI 6.42-12.58) were lost due to type 2 diabetes in 2022 in both sexes. This number is projected to increase to 9.5-13.5 million by 2060, mainly driven by the projected increase in the number of persons with type 2 diabetes. Conclusion: Type 2 diabetes-related productivity losses were shaped by SEP, sex and the future number of persons with the disease. PALYs lost declined with age and were predominantly driven by YPL.

after.authors: Aghaeeyan, A.; Goel, T.; Roswell, M.; Weitz, J. S.; Dushoff, J.
after.abstract: Heterogeneity in the expected number of secondary cases caused by infectors, R_c, has long been characterized using a skewed distribution with mean R_0, typically under the assumption of a fully susceptible population. We have recently shown that over the entire course of an SIR-modeled outbreak, the variation in R_c is constant and independent of R_0. Here, we extend that result by showing that the distribution of R_c across infectors over the course of a canonical SIR epidemic is precisely the standard exponential distribution, corresponding to a mean-one geometric distribution of realized infections in the canonical stochastic version. This result is exact in the limit of a small initial infection, and also requires a long-time limit in the case of persistent outbreaks. This result also applies to extensions of the model that allow immune waning and changes in R_0 across time (or as a function of susceptible density), but only if the infectious period remains exponentially distributed. The distribution of R_c, varies with R_0 when the generation-interval distribution is not exponential. Our findings highlight the critical role of the infectious period distribution in shaping the long-term outcomes of an outbreak.

after.title: Preprint: The longitudinal course of borderline personality disorder: Symptomatology, psychosocial functioning, and factors associated with long-term outcomes
after.authors: Seitz, K. I.; Zimmermann, J.; Kramer, L.; Hashagen, P.; Neukel, C.; Schmahl, C.; Bertsch, K.; Herpertz, S. C.
after.abstract: Objective: Longitudinal studies have transformed the understanding of borderline personality disorder (BPD), demonstrating substantial improvement over time. However, seminal findings have largely originated from U.S. cohorts. This study examined the long-term course of BPD and baseline factors associated with clinical and functional outcomes in a large German clinical cohort. Methods: Participants with a lifetime DSM-IV diagnosis of BPD (N=410) were assessed at baseline, with follow-up assessments conducted after a mean interval of 8.3 years (SD=1.8; range, 5.3-12.0). Changes in categorical diagnosis, dimensional symptom severity, psychosocial functioning, and healthcare utilization were examined using clinician-administered interviews and self-report measures. Baseline factors associated with follow-up outcomes were assessed after adjustment for baseline levels. Results: Follow-up assessments were completed by 186 participants (45.4%); attrition was weakly selective. Among participants with current BPD at baseline, 56.9% no longer met diagnostic criteria according to a 12-month assessment window. Dimensional symptom severity declined substantially across clinician-rated and self-report measures, although individual differences remained partially preserved over time. Psychosocial functioning showed more limited improvement, with 29.5% fulfilling a cross-sectional analogue of recovery including symptomatic remission, employment or education, and a stable partnership. Higher baseline self-reported BPD symptom severity and emotion dysregulation consistently indicated less favorable long-term clinical outcomes, whereas childhood maltreatment, comorbid mental disorders, and further baseline characteristics were not significant predictors. Conclusions: BPD shows substantial long-term improvement, but psychosocial recovery often lags behind symptomatic remission. These findings highlight the importance of treatment approaches that address functioning and quality of life in addition to symptom reduction.

after.authors: Pradeepkumar, N. A.; Green Snyder, L.; Trost, B.; Fernandez, B. A.; Shu, C. A.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Center for Genetic Epidemiology, Division of Epidemiology and Genetics, Department of Population and Public Health Sciences, Keck School of Medicine, University
after.abstract: Background: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition characterized by social communication difficulties and restricted, repetitive behaviors. While machine learning has been widely applied in autism research, few studies have predicted continuous autism severity measures such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule Calibrated Severity Score (ADOS CSS). We evaluated behavioral and genetic predictors of ADOS CSS across ADOS modules. Methods: Participants from the Simons Simplex Collection who completed ADOS Modules 1, 2, or 3 were included. Behavioral questionnaire data and gene-level measures of loss-of-function intolerance (pLI, LOEUF) and brain-expression specificity (pExt) were used to train 12 machine learning models separately for each module. Performance was evaluated using mean absolute error (MAE), Pearson correlation (r), and SHAP analyses. Results: Ensemble-based models achieved the strongest performance across modules. In Module 1, adding genetic predictors improved Random Forest performance (MAE 1.189 to 1.051; r 0.204 to 0.340). Module 2 achieved the highest overall performance, with XGBoost reaching r {approx} 0.49 and MAE = 1.010. SHAP analyses showed that genetic predictors contributed most strongly in Module 1, whereas predictions for Module 3 were driven primarily by verbal, behavioral, and social-cognitive features. Conclusions: Integrating genetic and behavioral features improved ADOS CSS prediction, particularly in children with limited expressive language. Genetic information was most informative in Module 1, while behavioral and social-cognitive measures became increasingly important in later developmental stages, consistent with evidence that genetic burden is more strongly associated with greater developmental impairment.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Partitioning lifespan inequality in hierarchical study designs with an application to global healthy longevity

after.title: Preprint: Partitioning lifespan inequality in hierarchical study designs with an application to global healthy longevity
after.authors: Caswell, H.
after.abstract: Background: Demographic inequality arises from two sources: heterogeneity among individuals subject to different rates, and stochastic variation among individuals subject to identical rates. Partitioning lifespan inequality into these components has been limited to heterogeneity in single factors or, very recently, factorial study designs with multiple factors. Methods for hierarchical designs have been lacking. Objectives: The goal of this paper is to present a generally applicable method to partition inequality of lifespan (and other demographic outcomes) into components within and between levels in a hierarchical study design. Methods: The analysis treats a heterogeneous population as a mixture distribution. Inequality is measured by the variance and partitioned into components between groups (e.g., geographical or economic regions), between sub-groups within groups (e.g., countries within regions), and stochasticity within sub-groups. The method is applied to global inequality in healthy longevity, using data for 194 countries from the Global Burden of Disease study, divided into four regions according to the World Bank income categories and into countries within each region. Results are compared for flat and population-weighted mixing distributions. Results: The protocol for variance partitioning in hierarchical study designs provides variance among regions, among countries within regions, and within countries. It extends naturally to multiple levels (e.g., states within countries) and to factorial components (e.g., regions defined by combinations of income and education). When applied to global healthy longevity, the dominant source of inequality is stochastic variation within countries, which accounts for 85\%-95\% of the overall inequality. The population-weighted mixing distribution reduces the contribution of between-group variance. Contribution: Some of the largest demographic data sets have a hierarchical organization. The methods presented here make it possible to partition inequality, measured by variance, in such studies.

after.authors: Greene, H.; Endres, K.; Sanvura, P.; Bisimwa, J.-C.; Williams, C.; Perin, J.; Bengehya, J.; Kulondwa, J. C.; Namunesha, A.; Felicien, W.; Maheshe, G.; Cirhuza Cikomola, J.; Mwishingo, A.; Bisimwa, L.; Dimitrova, A.; Caulfield, L.; George, C. M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health
after.abstract: Background: Evidence-informed anticipatory action is critical to mitigate the health impacts of extreme weather events. This randomized controlled trial (RCT) investigated the impact of the WASHmobile hygiene and water treatment program on anemia during extreme weather in east-ern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Methods: The WASHmobile RCT enrolled participants in Bukavu, DRC, from November 2021 to December 2022 (NCT05166850). Anemia was classified by WHO thresholds. CHIRPS data was used to calculate Standardized Precipitation Indices (SPI). Findings: Among 1,208 participants, 68% (822/1208) were anemic. Extreme wet (SPI-1[≥]2.0) (odds ratio (OR) 2.29; 95% CI 1.03, 5.11), severe wet (1.5[≤]SPI-1<2) (OR 3.25; CI 1.53, 6.93), and moderate drought conditions (-1.5 < SPI-1[≤] -1.0) (OR = 2.09; CI 1.28, 3.40) over the prior month were associated with significantly higher odds of anemia. In the standard arm, anemia was sig-nificantly higher during extreme wet conditions compared to near-normal conditions (78% vs. 62%, p=0.0496), whereas a non-significant decrease was observed in the WASHmobile arm (64% vs. 69%, p=0.55). Consistent with this, significant effect modification was observed between extreme wet conditions and WASHmobile delivery on anemia prevalence (multiplicative interaction p=0.044). These findings informed the design of the WASHmobile anticipatory action framework where pre-defined climate triggers activate an early warning system for anemia prevention. Interpretation: Extreme and severe wet conditions and moderate drought were associated with higher odds of anemia. WASHmobile presents a potential climate-resilient intervention to reduce anemia during extreme weather.

after.authors: Kit, A.; Miyazaki, A.; Kitano, N.; Okawachi, T.; Astuti, A. W.; Honda, S.
after.abstract: Background: Acceptance of corporal punishment and other harmful behaviors toward children may persist even among young adults without childhood maltreatment experiences. Objective: To identify factors associated with the acceptability of corporal punishment and related harmful behaviors toward children among university students without childhood maltreatment experiences, and to examine whether these associations differ across types of harmful behavior. Participants and Setting: An online cross-sectional survey was conducted at four Japanese universities in June 2024. Of 699 students analyzed, 568 reported no childhood maltreatment experiences. Methods: Participants rated the acceptability of 22 behaviors as discipline. Exploratory factor analysis identified three subfactors: neglect and psychological maltreatment, harsh physically aggressive behaviors, and less severe aggressive behaviors. Multivariable linear regression analyses were conducted among students without childhood maltreatment experiences. Higher scores indicated lower acceptance. Results: More egalitarian gender-role attitudes (B = 1.40, p = .001) and less frequent school-based physical violence experiences (B = 1.49, p = .024) were associated with lower overall acceptance of corporal punishment and related harmful behaviors. Associated factors differed across subfactors. Witnessing psychological violence, learning about child rearing, and enrollment in health, welfare, or rehabilitation-related faculties were associated with lower acceptance of less severe aggressive behaviors. Conclusions: Factors associated with acceptability differed across types of harmful behavior, even among students without childhood maltreatment experiences. These findings suggest the importance of prevention education addressing gender-role attitudes, recognition of harmful disciplinary practices, and child development. Educational opportunities throughout adolescence and young adulthood may help promote attitudes that reject violence against children.

after.title: Preprint: Within-scan MRI signal and texture in Alzheimer disease: a multicohort study
after.authors: Han, W.; Han, H.-J. S.; Kim, D.-J.; Yoon, B. C.
after.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Conventional MRI contains tissue signal and texture information beyond regional volume, but acquisition variability limits their comparability. We evaluated within-scan signal and texture analyses for estimating contemporaneous cognition and amyloid/tau burden in Alzheimer's disease (AD) beyond volumetry. METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 2,437 baseline datasets from ADNI3, ADNI4, MCSA, SCAN/CLARiTI, and OASIS-3. SynthSeg defined regions for T1-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) measurements. Within-scan regional-to-rest log ratios (WSRLR) were compared with scanner-matched, cross-fitted cognitively normal (CN) references. Texture analysis used three-dimensional gray-level co-occurrence matrices (GLCM). Covariate-adjusted rank models examined associations; ADNI3-trained ridge, elastic-net, gradient-boosting, and TabPFN-v2 models were tested externally. RESULTS: Moderate-to-strong correlations were observed between regional signal changes assessed using WSRLR vs. CN-reference (cohort median regional rho=0.504-0.890; n=2,314). Lower entorhinal FLAIR WSRLR and greater entropy were associated with AD dementia adjusted for volume, while opposite correlations were observed with the hippocampus (all q<0.001). Greater entorhinal FLAIR entropy correlated with lower Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores (r=-0.198 and -0.098, respectively; both q<0.001). Lower entorhinal FLAIR WSRLR and T1 cluster shade were associated with higher regional tau uptake beyond volume and diagnosis (r=-0.146 and -0.205; both q<=0.010). Adding entorhinal and hippocampal signal and texture significantly improved pooled external MoCA (n=868) and MMSE (n=551) prediction in three of four models. DISCUSSION: Within-scan signal and texture demonstrated AD-related regional associations and improved prediction of contemporaneous cognitive performance beyond volumetry. Prospective validation is needed to evaluate their potential value in opportunistic dementia screening.

METHODS: We retrospectively analyzed 2,437 baseline datasets from ADNI3, ADNI4, MCSA, SCAN/CLARiTI, and OASIS-3. SynthSeg defined regions for T1-weighted and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) measurements. Within-scan regional-to-rest log ratios (WSRLR) were compared with scanner-matched, cross-fitted cognitively normal (CN) references. Texture analysis used three-dimensional gray-level co-occurrence matrices (GLCM). Covariate-adjusted rank models examined associations; ADNI3-trained ridge, elastic-net, gradient-boosting, and TabPFN-v2 models were tested externally. RESULTS: Moderate-to-strong correlations were observed between regional signal changes assessed using WSRLR vs. CN-reference (cohort median regional rho=0.504-0.890; n=2,314). Lower entorhinal FLAIR WSRLR and greater entropy were associated with AD dementia adjusted for volume, while opposite correlations were observed with the hippocampus (all q<0.001). Greater entorhinal FLAIR entropy correlated with lower Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores (r=-0.198 and -0.098, respectively; both q<0.001). Lower entorhinal FLAIR WSRLR and T1 cluster shade were associated with higher regional tau uptake beyond volume and diagnosis (r=-0.146 and -0.205; both q<=0.010). Adding entorhinal and hippocampal signal and texture significantly improved pooled external MoCA (n=868) and MMSE (n=551) prediction in three of four models. DISCUSSION: Within-scan signal and texture demonstrated AD-related regional associations and improved prediction of contemporaneous cognitive performance beyond volumetry. Prospective validation is needed to evaluate their potential value in opportunistic dementia screening.

after.title: Preprint: Individualized Atypicality of Structure-Function Configuration Marks Subthreshold Depression in Adolescents
after.authors: Wang, R.; Guo, Q.; Lan, Z.; Wu, S.; Liu, W. V.; Leong, C.; Gao, W.; Zeng, J.; Zeng, X.; Myachykov, A.; Chen, J.; Yuan, Z.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Centre for Cognitive and Brain Sciences, Institute of Artificial Intelligence and Brain Sciences, University of Macau, Macau SAR, China; Department of Public He
after.abstract: Background: Subthreshold depression (StD) in adolescence represents a critical state preceding major depressive disorder, yet its neurobiological substrates remain poorly characterized. Conventional structure-function coupling rely on DTI tractography, which produces non-isomorphic matrices and unstable single-subject estimates, limiting their clinical utility. We developed a novel isomorphic and multi-omics framework to quantify individualized structure-function configurations and tested whether adolescents with StD show reproducible deviations from a group-mean reference in a validation sample. Methods: We integrated five structural (cortical thickness, mean curvature, sulcal depth, fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity) and five functional (ReHo, ALFF, CBF, local and global connectivity strength) features to construct regional SIND-FIND configurations using symmetric KL divergence in a discovery-validation design (N = 131). Individual typicality scores were defined as the correspondence between each participant's regional configuration profile and HC reference (Leave one out). The score has undergone parallel validations using conventional SC-FC coupling, molecular alignment (PET/AHBA), and behavioral correlations. Results: Group-mean configuration maps were spatially correlated across samples ({rho} = .93, pspin < .001). StD participants showed lower typicality than HC (F(1,94) = 8.73, p = .004); the conventional SC-FC comparison was not significant (F(1,92) = 3.31, p = .072). Regional differences involved frontoparietal and salience regions and aligned with PET (r = .55, pspin < .001) and AHBA (r = .47, pspin = .003) maps. After covariate adjustment, typicality correlated with SCL-90 ({rho} = -.262, q = .013), SDS ({rho} = -.234, q = .022), ISI ({rho} = -.296, q = .012) and PSQI ({rho} = -.288, q = .012; BH-FDR across five scales); coupling tracked depressive but not sleep symptoms (ISI {rho} = -.161, q = .124). Within validation StD participants, SCL-90 remained negatively associated with typicality ({rho} = -.42, p = .023). Conclusion: Our isomorphic, multimodal framework captures coordinated structures-function deviation in adolescent StD with greater group-effect sensitivity than conventional SC-FC coupling, together with regional specificity, molecular spatial alignment, and behavioral relevance. Configuration typicality, defined relative to an HC group-mean reference, may serve as an individual-level marker of organizational deviation during adolescence, pending larger, demographic stratified samples.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Pulmonary Medicine, The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, Houston, Texas, USA
after.abstract: Research Question Among adult first allogeneic HCT recipients sampled in a nested case-control study, how did bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome (BOS) affect institutional cost trajectories compared to extrapulmonary chronic graft-versus-host disease (cGVHD) and no cGVHD, and can this information guide cost-effective implementation of home spirometry? Study Design and Methods We linked clinical, pulmonary function test (PFT), vital-status, and institutional billing data for 308 patients from a nested case-control study: 111 with BOS, 132 with cGVHD without BOS, and 65 without cGVHD. Comparator patients were matched to BOS cases by age (within 10 years), transplantation era (5-year intervals), and time since HCT (within 1 month). Monthly costs from M-6 through M+6 were standardized to 2024 US dollars using CPI-U Medical Care. Gaussian identity-link generalized estimating equations (GEE) modeled clinical group, month, and the group-by-month interaction to calculate within-group pre/post and difference-in-differences (DiD) tests. BOS surveillance analyses evaluated clinic PFT frequency, FEV trajectories, and home-spirometry break-even and net monetary benefit (NMB) scenarios, incorporating projected monitoring costs, avoided BOS-associated costs, and the monetary value of health benefits. Results Mean monthly cost fell after index in patients without cGVHD by $7,582 (95% CI, -$13,378 to -$1,786; p = 0.01), but not in cGVHD (-$5,768; p = 0.08) or BOS (+$4,470; p = 0.23). The BOS trajectory was $12,052/month less favorable than no cGVHD (95% CI, $2,700-$21,404; p = 0.01), a six-month differential of $72,313. The BOS-vs-cGVHD DiD was $10,238/month in BOS (p = 0.04). Antecedent decline was documented in 40/108 BOS cases (37.0%), a median of 268 days before diagnosis. Each additional clinic PFT/year was associated with higher detection odds (OR, 2.38; 95% CI, 1.41-4.02; p = 0.001). Among BOS cases in the parent cohort, undetected impairment was not significantly associated with geographic proximity to comprehensive cancer centers or socioeconomic vulnerability. At an assumed BOS frequency of 5%, targeted home monitoring would need to prevent 44.7% of the modeled six-month BOS-associated costs among additionally detected cases to offset monitoring expenses, whereas universal monitoring would require 104.2% cost reduction and therefore could not break even. Under 30% mitigation and 0.10 assumed annual utility gain, targeted-monitoring NMB was -$54,897 at 5%, +$70,206 at 10%, and +$195,309 at 15% BOS frequency. Interpretation BOS was associated with a higher post-index institutional-cost trajectory than no extrapulmonary cGVHD and no cGVHD. More frequent PFT surveillance, but not geographic or socioeconomic access, was associated with detection of early declines. Targeted home monitoring became economically favorable only under selected higher-risk assumptions.

after.title: Preprint: Etiological profile of digital necrosis in internal medicine: a retrospective study of 44 cases
after.authors: Toujani, S.; Belhaj Hassen, Y.; El Ouni, A.; Hnen, Y.; Abdelkefi, C.; Tekaya, A.; Larbi, T.; Meddeb, Z.; Hamzaoui, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Internal Medicine, Mongi Slim University Hospital, La Marsa, Tunis
after.abstract: Background. We aimed to describe the etiological profile of digital necrosis in an internal medicine setting and to assess the respective diagnostic yield of the clinical and paraclinical components of the etiological work-up. Methods. We conducted a descriptive, retrospective, single-centre study of 44 patients admitted for one or more digital necroses to an internal medicine department between 1997 and 2022. For each patient, clinical data and documented complementary investigations were reviewed; an item was considered contributory when its positivity oriented the etiological diagnosis. Results. The 44 patients comprised 23 women and 21 men (male-to-female ratio 0.91), with a mean age of 51 (SD 14) years. Raynaud's phenomenon preceded the necrosis in 36.4% of cases. The necrosis involved at least two fingers in 72.7% of cases, the index finger being most frequently affected (56.8%); associated toe necrosis was present in 18.1% of cases. Connective tissue diseases were the leading cause (29.5%), dominated by systemic sclerosis, followed by thromboangiitis obliterans (18.1%), malignancy (15.9%) and vasculitis (9.1%). The necrosis revealed the underlying disease in 35 patients (79.5%), and the work-up remained inconclusive in 11.3% of cases. History taking and physical examination were contributory in 61.4% and 43.2% of cases, respectively, ahead of biological (37.1%), morphological (40%) and histopathological (36.4%) investigations. Conclusions. The etiological profile of digital necrosis in internal medicine is dominated by connective tissue diseases, the necrosis frequently revealing the underlying disorder. History taking and physical examination provide the highest diagnostic yield and should guide a targeted prescription of investigations. Keywords: digital necrosis; etiology; connective tissue disease; Raynaud's phenomenon.

after.abstract: Background: Doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxyPEP) reduces the incidence of bacterial sexually transmitted infections, but its impact on antimicrobial susceptibility among bystander bacteria remains unclear. Objectives: To assess changes in susceptibility to doxycycline among rectal Escherichia coli after 6 months of doxyPEP. Secondary objectives assessed susceptibility for other classes of antimicrobials and in other species. Patients and methods: Single-centre, open-label, single-arm trial at an HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis clinic in Belgium. Participants used doxycycline 200mg within 72h after condomless sex for 180 days. Anorectal swabs and oral rinse samples were collected at baseline and day 180. Susceptibility was assessed by disc diffusion on six colonies per species. Differences in inhibition-zone diameters were analysed using censored Bayesian mixed-effects Gaussian regression. Results: Seventy-nine participants were enrolled, 73 completed day 180. Among rectal isolates, cefixime inhibition-zone diameters decreased in E. coli and Klebsiella spp., other estimates were imprecise. Among oral isolates, inhibition-zone diameters decreased for doxycycline and azithromycin in streptococci, staphylococci and commensal Neisseria spp.; ceftriaxone and cefixime in commensal Neisseria spp.; and ciprofloxacin and penicillin in staphylococci and commensal Neisseria spp. Ceftriaxone inhibition-zone diameters increased in oral streptococci. Sensitivity analyses were broadly consistent. Twenty-five participants experienced drug-related adverse events, none serious. Conclusions: Six months of doxyPEP was associated with reduced susceptibility to doxycycline and several other antimicrobials, predominantly among oral bacteria. Rectal findings were less precise apart from reduced cefixime susceptibility in E. coli and Klebsiella spp. These findings support further studies of DoxyPEP and bystander selection across multiple bacterial taxa and antimicrobial classes.

after.title: Preprint: Exercise misinformation in fitness content targeted at women on Instagram and TikTok: a cross-sectional content analysis of 6,982 posts
after.authors: Schlegel, I.; Ozakinci, G.
after.abstract: Objectives. To quantify exercise misinformation in female targeted exercise content on Instagram and TikTok, determine whether content textually targeted at women carries higher rates of misinformation, and compare content from creators self identifying as ethnic minority with other content. Methods. Cross sectional content analysis of 6,982 posts collected March to June 2026 by manual browsing, which captured on screen and caption text, and automated collection, which captured captions only. Text was coded for claim accuracy, textual female targeting and creator characteristics, with large language model assisted coding verified against an independent human coder. Effects were estimated by logistic regression using adjustment sets from a pre specified causal diagram, with creator clustered standard errors. Results. Of 6,524 posts, 2,447 made an assessable exercise claim, of which 600 (24.5%, 95% CI 22.8 to 26.2) contained misinformation. Textually female targeted content carried more than twice the odds of misinformation compared with untargeted content (OR 2.06, 95% CI 1.58 to 2.70), particularly wholly inaccurate content. The effect was OR 4.00 (2.41 to 6.66) where on screen text was captured and 1.04 (0.73 to 1.49) where only captions were (interaction p < 0.001). Content from creators self identifying as ethnic minority carried less misinformation (OR 0.69, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.92). Conclusion. 24.5% of fitness posts making a verifiable claim contained misinformation, and content directed at women had higher rates where the full written text could be read. Posts naming a body part were most likely to be inaccurate, giving clinicians and public health communicators a teachable marker of misinformation.
